would you say it is safe to submit this text for a college assignment: John Hersey’s “Hiroshima” presents a moving and thought-provoking narrative that recounts the events surrounding the atomic bombing of the Japanese city of Hiroshima in August 1945. Hersey’s narrative is centered around six survivors of the blast, allowing for a powerful examination of the devastating aftermath of the bombing. By recounting the experiences of these individuals from their own unique perspectives, Hersey compellingly highlights the inhumane effects that resulted from the deployment of this destructive weapon. This review critically examines the book’s impact on the reader’s position on the dropping of the atomic bomb, the subsequent arms race, and whether focusing on the experiences of individuals who survived the bomb, rather than the leaders who developed and used it, makes a difference.
Right from the opening of the book, Hersey enthralls readers by plunging them headlong into the personal stories of six survivors, evoking a strong sense of empathy and compassion towards these ordinary individuals who had to endure the aftermath of the tragic event. Through vividly detailed accounts of their experiences and heartfelt feelings, readers are prompted to possibly rethink their stance on the use of nuclear arms as well as the resulting arms race (Hersey). These stories give a human face to the conflict and reveal the devastating consequences rather than just abstract concepts or statistics.
When evaluating the logic and rationale behind detonating the atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Hersey suggests that prioritizing survivors’ accounts rather than the leaders who instigated the bomb’s use can lead to different conclusions. Through their firsthand perspectives and an intimate portrayal of the tragedy’s aftermath, Hersey’s narrative invites readers to ponder the ethical implications of the bombing decision by challenging them to consider whether the decision was genuinely justified. By zeroing in on the six individuals, Hersey creates a connection between the reader and the people in Hiroshima, encouraging readers to see more than just a strategic military move, but a decision that affected the lives of countless innocent people.
By approaching the bombing of Hiroshima from the standpoint of survivors and their stories, “Hiroshima” provides an alternate and valuable perspective on the event and the resulting arms race. While it is crucial for historians to give attention to political leaders, military personnel, and strategic reasoning when examining the event, it is equally crucial not to overlook the experiences of the individuals who were deeply and directly affected, for it is their experiences that offer a significantly different and overlooked angle of the tragedy. Additionally, the stories of these six individuals may lead readers to question the necessity of the arms race and to ponder the potential ramifications of continued nuclear warfare.
In conclusion, “Hiroshima” provides an essential perspective on the consequences of the dropping of the atomic bomb and the subsequent arms race. By focusing on the experiences of the survivors rather than the leaders who deployed the bomb, Hersey encourages the reader to reconsider their stance on nuclear weapons and the arms race’s necessity. In an era in which the threat of nuclear weapons remains ever-present, books that examine the past with sensitivity and empathy, like “Hiroshima,” become more vital than ever. Encouraging readers to consider the human impact of war and the development of weapons of mass destruction could ultimately prove essential in avoiding the repetition of history and promoting a more peaceful world.

The research proposal is below
Introduction
Music events form an increasingly significant component of the cultural and entertainment landscape in many cities worldwide, offering not only entertainment but also potential socio-economic benefits to their host communities (Gursoy et al., 2017). Lagos, a vibrant metropolis and the economic hub of Nigeria, has witnessed a surge in the hosting of various local and international music events in recent years, ranging from concerts and festivals to music awards ceremonies (Adeaga & Oladipo, 2020). These events have contributed to the popularity of Lagos as a cultural destination while providing opportunities for revenue generation, job creation, and local community development (Gibson & Connell, 2016).

Despite the perceived significance of music events within the city, existing literature has not sufficiently explored the diverse socio-economic impacts emanating from these events in the context of Lagos. This gap in research presents the need for a comprehensive investigation into the consequences of music events in relation to the city’s economic growth, social well-being, and cultural development. Therefore, this study aims to explore the socio-economic impacts of music events in Lagos, with a focus on identifying the various stakeholders involved and the potential opportunities and challenges faced by the city in leveraging music events for sustainable development. This research will contribute to an enhanced understanding of the role of music events in urban development and provide valuable insights for policymakers, event organizers, and the musical community in Lagos.

Research statement: This study seeks to investigate the socio-economic impacts of music events in Lagos, examining the relationship between these events and local community development while highlighting key implications for policy and practice.

Aim and Objectives: The aim of this study is to explore the socio-economic impacts of music events in Lagos and understand their role in the city’s development. 
To achieve this aim, the associated objectives are:

1. To examine the different types of music events hosted in Lagos and their contribution to the local economy.
2. To identify key stakeholders involved in organizing and benefiting from music events.
3. To evaluate the social and cultural impacts of music events on local communities and the city’s identity
4. To provide recommendations to effectively capitalize on music events for promoting sustainable urban development in Lagos


Literature Review
The socio-economic impacts of music events have been the focus of numerous studies in the field of cultural and event tourism (Connell & Gibson, 2015; Gursoy et al., 2017). One key aspect of this research domain is the economic impact of music events, commonly measured through indicators such as direct expenditure, revenue generation, job creation, and multiplier effects (Gibson & Connell, 2016). Several scholars noted the positive economic contributions of music events, ranging from large-scale international festivals to smaller local concerts. For instance, Gursoy et al. (2017) found that music events significantly contribute to a city’s GDP, create job opportunities, and attract additional spending from visitors, thereby enhancing the local economy. In the context of Lagos, Adeaga & Oladipo (2020) reported that the hosting of music events has led to an increase in tourist arrivals and contributed to a growing cultural tourism market in the city.

Several studies have also examined the multiple ways in which music events benefit local communities and contribute to cultural development (Smith, 2014; Waitt, 2018). For example, music events have been associated with fostering social cohesion and a sense of belonging among local residents (Connell & Gibson, 2015) and have served as vehicles for cultural exchange and the promotion of local cultures and identities (Chalip, 2017). Moreover, music events can act as catalysts for urban regeneration and the revitalization of public spaces, offering opportunities to enhance the quality of urban environments and improve the attractiveness of a city for residents and tourists alike (Frost & Laing, 2018). Yet,  these events can give rise to negative consequences, Like traffic congestion, noise pollution, and the displacement of local communities (Smith, 2014). Furthermore, the temporary nature of some events may limit their long-term benefits for host cities, while the high costs associated with organizing large-scale events may outweigh the potential economic gains (Connell & Gibson, 2015). Therefore, a balanced and comprehensive understanding is essential when examining the socio-economic impacts of music events (Gursoy et al., 2017).

In order to provide a holistic assessment of these impacts, studies have employed various research methodologies, including qualitative case studies, surveys, and interviews with stakeholders, as well as quantitative analyses of economic indicators (Connell & Gibson, 2015). Partnerships between researchers, event organizers, policymakers, and local communities have been emphasized in order to generate context-sensitive knowledge that can inform practical decision-making (Smith, 2014; Waitt, 2018). Although previous research has advanced our understanding of the socio-economic impacts of music events, much of this work has been conducted in Western countries, while the African context (and Lagos in particular) remains considerably underexplored (Adeaga & Oladipo, 2020). Given the unique characteristics of Lagos, including its status as a major cultural hub in Sub-Saharan Africa, the findings from Western-based studies may not be fully applicable to this context (Gibson & Connell, 2016).

Moreover, emerging research attests to the diversity and complexity of the impacts of music events, indicating the need for context-specific analyses that take into account the different types of events, their scope and scale, and the local socio-economic conditions (Connell & Gibson, 2015; Gursoy et al., 2017). As Lagos continues to expand its music events scene, there is a pressing need for research that guides the city’s efforts to capitalize on these events in a sustainable and inclusive manner (Adeaga & Oladipo, 2020).

Research Methodology
To explore the socio-economic impacts of music events in Lagos, a quantitative research design will be deployed, which involves the collection and analysis of numerical data (Creswell, 2018). This approach was adopted due to its ability to provide a structured and objective assessment of the relationship between music events and their perceived socio-economic impacts. The choice of quantitative research is also guided by the need to obtain a clear understanding of the economic contributions of music events through the use of specific tools that will be used for analyzing the data. Below is a Ghannt chart for the proposed research





Research philosophy and approach:The research philosophy underpinning this study subscribes to pragmatism, acknowledging that both objective and subjective realities influence the socio-economic impacts of music events and the experiences of various stakeholders (Saunders et al., 2019). Consequently, the researcher adopts an abductive approach, moving back and forth between empirical data and theoretical insights to generate a more profound understanding of the subject (Nunkoo, 2018).

Sampling: The targeted population for this research includes event organizers, local venue owners, musicians, policymakers, and local community members in Lagos. This research will use a probability sampling technique to select participants who have knowledge or experience with music events in Lagos (Flick, 2018). A sample of not less than 500 respondents will be targeted for the survey, and these will be randomly selected from social media and professional networks.

Data collection: Primary data will be collected using an online survey, administered to event organizers, venue owners, musicians, policymakers, and members of the general public in Lagos. The survey will comprise closed-ended questions to assess participants’ perceptions of the economic, social, and cultural impacts of music events in Lagos. Data will be collected using Google forms and will be analyzed using Excel. Secondary data will also be collected from various sources, such as government reports, industry statistics, and event evaluations, to complement and triangulate the primary data (Saunders et al., 2019).

Data analysis: The quantitative data from the surveys will be analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multiple regression analysis to draw relationships between music events and their perceived socio-economic impacts (Field, 2013). Data analysis tools such as SPSS and Excel would be employed in analyzing the data. 

Ethical considerations: This research will adhere to established ethical guidelines concerning anonymity, confidentiality, and voluntary participation (Sanders et al., 2019). Informed consent will be sought from all participants, and they will be informed of their right to withdraw from the study at any time without repercussions. The collected data will be securely stored and only used for the purposes of this research (Silver & Woolf, 2018). Approval for the study will be sought from the internal institutional review board (IRB) before data collection commences.

Conclusion
The findings of this research have the potential to offer practical recommendations for policymakers, event organizers, and the musical community in leveraging music events for sustainable urban development and enhancing the city’s position as an emerging cultural destination in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Metalearning describes that learning is structured into Concepts, Facts and Processes. Concepts are ideas that you need to understand in flexible ways in order for them to be useful. Math and physics, for example, are both subjects that lean heavily toward concepts.
In general, if something needs to be understood, not just memorized, you will list it as a concept. Facts are anything that suffices if you can remember
them at all. You don’t need to understand them too deeply, so
long as you can recall them in the right situations. Languages, for
instance, are full of facts about vocabulary, pronunciation, and, to
a lesser extent, grammar. Even concept-heavy subjects usually
have some facts. For example, If you’re learning calculus, you will need to
deeply understand how derivatives work, but it may be sufficient
to memorize some trigonometric identities. In general if anything needs to be memorized, you will list it as a fact. Procedures are actions that need to be performed and may not involve much conscious thinking at all. Learning to ride a

In assessing the appropriate stance of monetary policy, the Committee will continue to monitor the implications of incoming information for the economic outlook. The Committee would be prepared to adjust the stance of monetary policy as appropriate if risks emerge that could impede the attainment of the Committee's goals. Creating the course.

1.	Conduct Research:

- Create learner personas to guide the course design process and ensure that the courses cater to the unique needs of Nigerian university students and faculty.

2. Align with Project Stakeholders:
- Collaborate with subject matter experts, to ensure that the content of the courses is accurate, relevant, and up-to-date. These could include professors, industry professionals, or researchers in the fields. 
- Hold meeting with university administrators, instructors, and the Ed-tech startup team to establish common goals and expectations.
- Hold regular meetings to discuss project progress, challenges, and opportunities and adjust course design accordingly.

- Develop design prototypes that are based on the Flipped Classroom Model, showing that students will review the lecture materials at home and engage in active learning activities during the class by drafting course materials, learning activities and share them with stakeholders and potential learners for feedback.
- Test and iterate on the course design based on the feedback received, ensuring a learner-centered and responsive approach.

- Develop a well-structured course roadmap that outlines course objectives, week-by-week activities, assignments, and assessments.

Designing The course.
1. Develop Effective Digital Content:
- Utilize a variety of engaging multimedia formats (written, audio, video, and interactive elements) to appeal to various learning styles and preferences, in chunks. 
- Integrate hands-on activities, case studies, and real-world examples to ensure the course content is practical and useful for students.

2. Leverage the Flipped Classroom Model:
- Design online asynchronous activities that encourage students to absorb new concepts at their own pace before the synchronous (live) sessions, such as a combination of  videos, audio recordings, readings, discussions, forums, simulations and quizzes to create a more engaging and effective learning experience.
- Foster active learning in synchronous sessions (e.g., online video conferences) by facilitating discussions, encouraging problem-solving, and providing opportunities for group collaboration.
- Begin by organizing course materials into modules or units, providing a clear and linear structure. Design courses to progressively increase in complexity and difficulty, building on previously learned concepts. The design should encourage peer-to-peer learning and grading, group discussions, and projects to enhance collaboration, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills among students. Facilitate online forums and class-wide discussions to create a sense of community within the virtual classroom.

3. Design Assessments Aligned with Learning Goals:
- Develop assessment tools that accurately measure the progress and attainment of learning objectives.
- Use a mix of formative and summative assessments (e.g., quizzes, essays, projects, etc.) that not only evaluate learners’ knowledge but also facilitate continued learning.
- Develop rubrics to standardize the grading process and ensure fair evaluation for peer grading

4. Implement Continuous Improvement:
- Collect data from learners, stakeholders, and course performance metrics to determine the effectiveness of the courses and identify areas for improvement.
- Iterate on the course design based on data-driven insights and learner feedback.

If a Wyoming Corporation forms a North Carolina LLC to operate in North Carolina, the LLC will be considered a separate entity for tax purposes. As a result, the LLC will be subject to North Carolina state taxes on the income it earns in North Carolina, which includes income from sales, services, and tangible property within the state.

The Wyoming Corporation itself, as a separate entity, will still be subject to Wyoming state taxes on its income derived from Wyoming. However, it may be possible for the Wyoming Corporation to avoid double taxation by filing as an S corporation or by establishing a limited liability company (LLC) taxed as a partnership, in which case the profits and losses would pass through to the shareholders or members and be taxed only at the individual level.

It’s important to note that different states have different tax laws, and it’s important to comply with all applicable tax laws to avoid penalties and fines. To ensure proper compliance, it’s recommended to consult with a tax professional or accountant who is knowledgeable about the tax laws of both Wyoming and North Carolina and how they apply to your specific situation.

generate high quality slides to Top management of Department of social development for presentation by providing an Overview of international income support for children with disabilities  from the following: international income support for children with disabilities in the UK, Australia, Mexico, and Kenya:

United Kingdom (UK):
The Carer's Allowance (CA) is a state benefit in the UK that provides financial support to individuals who care for a disabled person. To be eligible for the Carer's Allowance, the caregiver must provide care for a minimum of 35 hours per week and meet certain income and eligibility requirements. The allowance is means-tested and provided by the UK government to individuals who care for someone receiving specific benefits. Carers receiving means-tested benefits are also entitled to additional payments known as Carer Premium or Additional Amount.
The Carer's Allowance is part of the UK's social security system and is governed by legislation such as the Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 and the Carer's Allowance Regulations 2002. However, there are critiques regarding its low payment level, restrictions on eligibility, lack of support for young carers, and administrative complexity.

Australia:
Australia provides income support to carers through the Carer Payment and Carer Allowance programs. The Carer Payment is an income-replacement allowance for carers who are unable to work outside the home due to their caregiving responsibilities. The Carer Allowance is a non-taxable supplement for carers who are already receiving another income support payment.
Eligibility criteria and payment amounts vary based on the individual circumstances of the carer and the person they are caring for. The primary legislation governing these programs is the Social Security Act of 1991, along with various guidelines and policies. The Carer Gateway program in Australia offers tailored supports and services to help carers manage their daily challenges, reduce stress, and plan for the future.

However, the Carer Payment and Carer Allowance have been criticized for their limited coverage, complex eligibility criteria, insufficient payment amounts, lack of flexibility, and limited access to support services.

Mexico:
The Prospera program in Mexico, formerly known as PROGRESA and Oportunidades, is a national conditional cash transfer (CCT) program aimed at reducing poverty and improving the well-being of vulnerable populations, including children with disabilities. The program uses cash transfers as incentives for parents to invest in their children's health and education, with the goal of breaking the cycle of intergenerational poverty.
Under the Prospera program, families with children with disabilities are eligible to receive higher cash transfers. The amount of financial assistance depends on the severity of the child's disability, with families with children with severe disabilities receiving higher amounts of support. The program also provides access to specialized health services, including rehabilitation services, medical consultations, and diagnostic tests, to children with disabilities enrolled in the program. Additionally, the program supports children with disabilities in accessing education services, such as special education programs and assistive technologies. It also offers social services like housing, transportation, and food assistance to families with children with disabilities.

The program collaborates with various government agencies and civil society organizations to provide these specialized services. It works with health institutions and service providers to ensure that children with disabilities receive the necessary care. It also partners with educational institutions and teachers to promote inclusive education and provide additional support for children with disabilities.

The Prospera program is governed by several policies and legislation, including the General Law of Social Development, Prospera Program Regulations, National Development Plan, General Health Law, and General Education Law. These legal frameworks outline the principles, objectives, eligibility criteria, and requirements for program participation. The program undergoes oversight and evaluation by government agencies such as the Ministry of Social Development, the National Council for the Evaluation of Social Development Policy, and the Federal Auditor's Office to monitor its operations, effectiveness, and efficiency in achieving its poverty reduction and well-being improvement objectives.

However, the program has faced criticisms similar to South Africa's Child Support Grant (CDG). Some of the issues raised include limited access to services, with concerns that many children with disabilities still struggle to access the support they need due to barriers such as lack of information or limited availability of services in certain regions. There are also concerns about the lack of data and evaluation on the impact of the Prospera program specifically for children with disabilities, making it challenging to assess its effectiveness and identify areas for improvement. Additionally, children with disabilities in Mexico often face stigma and discrimination, which can restrict their opportunities and access to services.

Kenya:
In Kenya, there are two income support programs aimed at supporting vulnerable populations and children with disabilities: the Cash Transfer Programme for Orphans and Vulnerable Children (OVC) and the Cash Transfer for Persons with Severe Disabilities (PWSD).
The Cash Transfer Programme for OVC was established in 2004 as part of the Social Protection (SP) framework in Kenya. The program provides financial and social support to the poorest households containing OVC, with a special focus on those affected by HIV/AIDS. The cash transfers are intended to be used for food, clothes, education, health services, and other essential needs. The primary goal of the program is to keep OVC within their families and communities and promote their development. The program's conditional and unconditional aspects depend on the beneficiaries' location and their access to education and health facilities. Beneficiary households are required to ensure the care and protection of OVC, including school attendance for eligible children and health center visits for younger children. Eligibility for the program is based on household poverty status and the presence of OVC aged 0-17 years with a deceased parent, chronically ill parent, or severe disability. The program is implemented in partnership with the government of Kenya, UNICEF, UK Department for International Development (DFID), Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA), and International Development Association (IDA). It is monitored and evaluated by constituency Social Assistance Committees (CSAC) and Location OVC Committees (LOC).

Another social assistance program in Kenya is the Cash Transfer for Persons with Severe Disabilities (PWSD). Launched in 2011, this program aims to enhance the livelihoods of individuals with severe disabilities and reduce the negative impact of disability on households. The program provides cash transfers to caregivers of adults and children with severe disabilities who require full-time support. The eligibility criteria include the need for permanent care, poverty status, non-enrollment in other cash transfer programs, and no receipt of pension or regular income. The PWSD program is implemented nationwide and covers beneficiaries in all counties. The cash transfers are delivered every two months through appointed payment agents.

Both the Cash Transfer Programme for OVC and the PWSD program in Kenya face several challenges and barriers. One major challenge is the lack of awareness among potential beneficiaries, which can be attributed to a lack of information, difficulties in accessing registration processes, and societal stigma and discrimination towards people with disabilities. Insufficient funding is also a significant barrier, limiting the number of beneficiaries and the level of support that can be provided. Inadequate disability assessment mechanisms have been highlighted, calling for a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of the needs of people with disabilities. Additionally, the poverty targeting applied to the PWSD program excludes a large proportion of people with disabilities who are in need of social protection.

In comparison to South Africa's Child Support Grant (CDG) program, the PWSD-CT program in Kenya faces greater challenges in terms of awareness, funding, and disability assessment. The CDG program in South Africa has been commended for its design and administrative management, suggesting that it may be more effective in reaching and supporting its intended beneficiaries.

In terms of their career, young people who decide to find work, rather than continue their studies, may progress more quickly. Secondly, the job market is becoming increasingly competitive, and sometimes there are hundreds of applicants for one position in a company. Young people who do not have qualifications from a university or college will not be able to compete.

Based on the following, guidelines on (PIRS) evaluation, provide  specific detailed examples of persons impairments, behaviour and functionality, ect. who has been diagnosed with Exacerbation of refractory major depressive disorder with severe anxiety. provide at least four examples for each rating scale (class) in each area of functional impairment: { https://www.sira.nsw.gov.au/resources-library/workers-compensation-resources/publications/health-professionals-for-workers-compensation/workers-compensation-guidelines-for-the-evaluation-of-permanent-impairment?result_64356_result_page=11&id=329613#table113  HomeResources libraryNSW workers compensation guidelines for the evaluation of permanent impairmentPsychiatric and psychological disorders
Psychiatric and psychological disorders
AMA5 Chapter 14 is excluded and replaced by this chapter. Before undertaking an impairment assessment, users of the Guidelines must be familiar with (in this order):

the Introduction in the Guidelines
chapters 1 and 2 of AMA5
the appropriate chapter(s) of the Guidelines for the body system they are assessing.
The Guidelines replace the psychiatric and psychological chapter in AMA5.

Introduction
11.1 This chapter lays out the method for assessing psychiatric impairment. The evaluation of impairment requires a medical examination.

11.2 Evaluation of psychiatric impairment is conducted by a psychiatrist who has undergone appropriate training in this assessment method.

11.3 Permanent impairment assessments for psychiatric and psychological disorders are only required where the primary injury is a psychological one. The psychiatrist needs to confirm that the psychiatric diagnosis is the injured worker’s primary diagnosis.

Diagnosis
11.4 The impairment rating must be based upon a psychiatric diagnosis (according to a recognised diagnostic system) and the report must specify the diagnostic criteria upon which the diagnosis is based. Impairment arising from any of the somatoform disorders (DSM IV TR, pp 485–511) are excluded from this chapter.

11.5 If pain is present as the result of an organic impairment, it should be assessed as part of the organic condition under the relevant table. This does not constitute part of the assessment of impairment relating to the psychiatric condition. The impairment ratings in the body organ system chapters in AMA5 make allowance for any accompanying pain.

11.6 It is expected that the psychiatrist will provide a rationale for the rating based on the injured worker’s psychiatric symptoms. The diagnosis is among the factors to be considered in assessing the severity and possible duration of the impairment, but is not the sole criterion to be used. Clinical assessment of the person may include information from the injured worker’s own description of his or her functioning and limitations, and from family members and others who may have knowledge of the person. Medical reports, feedback from treating professionals and the results of standardised tests – including appropriate psychometric testing performed by a qualified clinical psychologist and work evaluations – may provide useful information to assist with the assessment. Evaluation of impairment will need to take into account variations in the level of functioning over time. Percentage impairment refers to whole person impairment (WPI).

Permanent impairment
11.7 A psychiatric disorder is permanent if, in your clinical opinion, it is likely to continue indefinitely. Regard should be given to:

the duration of impairment
the likelihood of improvement in the injured worker’s condition
whether the injured worker has undertaken reasonable rehabilitative treatment
any other relevant matters.
Effects of treatment
11.8 Consider the effects of medication, treatment and rehabilitation to date. Is the condition stable? Is treatment likely to change? Are symptoms likely to improve? If the injured worker declines treatment, this should not affect the estimate of permanent impairment. The psychiatrist may make a comment in the report about the likely effect of treatment or the reasons for refusal of treatment.

Co-morbidity
11.9 Consider comorbid features (eg bi-polar disorder, personality disorder, substance abuse) and determine whether they are directly linked to the work-related injury, or whether they were pre-existing or unrelated conditions.

Pre-existing impairment
11.10 To measure the impairment caused by a work-related injury or incident, the psychiatrist must measure the proportion of WPI due to a pre-existing condition. Pre-existing impairment is calculated using the same method for calculating current impairment level. The assessing psychiatrist uses all available information to rate the injured worker’s pre-injury level of functioning in each of the areas of function. The percentage impairment is calculated using the aggregate score and median class score using the conversion table below. The injured worker’s current level of WPI% is then assessed, and the pre-existing WPI% is subtracted from their current level, to obtain the percentage of permanent impairment directly attributable to the work-related injury. If the percentage of pre-existing impairment cannot be assessed, the deduction is 1/10th of the assessed WPI.

Psychiatric impairment rating scale (PIRS)
11.11 Behavioural consequences of psychiatric disorder are assessed on six scales, each of which evaluates an area of functional impairment:

Self care and personal hygiene (Table 11.1) - Activities of daily living
Social and recreational activities (Table 11.2) - Activities of daily living
Travel (Table 11.3) - Activities of daily living
Social functioning (relationships) (Table 11.4)
Concentration, persistence and pace (Table 11.5)
Employability (Table 11.6).
11.12 Impairment in each area is rated using class descriptors. Classes range from 1 to 5, in accordance with severity. The standard form must be used when scoring the PIRS. The examples of activities are examples only. The assessing psychiatrist should take account of the person’s cultural background. Consider activities that are usual for the person’s age, sex and cultural norms.

Table 11.1: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - self care and personal hygiene
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population.
Class 2 Mild impairment: Able to live independently; looks after self adequately, although may look unkempt occasionally; sometimes misses a meal or relies on take-away food.
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Can’t live independently without regular support. Needs prompting to shower daily and wear clean clothes. Does not prepare own meals, frequently misses meals. Family member or community nurse visits (or should visit) 2-3 times per week to ensure minimum level of hygiene and nutrition.
Class 4 Severe impairment: Needs supervised residential care. If unsupervised, may accidentally or purposefully hurt self.
Class 5 Totally impaired: Needs assistance with basic functions, such as feeding and toileting.
Table 11.2: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - social and recreational activities
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population: regularly participates in social activities that are age, sex and culturally appropriate. May belong to clubs or associations and is actively involved with these.
Class 2 Mild impairment: Occasionally goes to such events eg without needing a support person, but does not become actively involved (eg dancing, cheering favourite team).
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Rarely goes out to such events, and mostly when prompted by family or close friend. Will not go out without a support person. Not actively involved, remains quiet and withdrawn.
Class 4 Severe impairment: Never leaves place of residence. Tolerates the company of family member or close friend, but will go to a different room or garden when others come to visit family or flat mate.
Class 5 Totally impaired: Cannot tolerate living with anybody, extremely uncomfortable when visited by close family member.
Table 11.3: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - travel
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population: Can travel to new environments without supervision.
Class 2 Mild impairment: Can travel without support person, but only in a familiar area such as local shops, visiting a neighbour.
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Cannot travel away from own residence without support person. Problems may e due to excessive anxiety or cognitive impairment.
Class 4 Severe impairment: Finds it extremely uncomfortable to leave own residence even with trusted person.
Class 5 Totally impaired: May require two or more persons to supervise when travelling.
Table 11.4: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - social functioning
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population: No difficulty in forming and sustaining relationships (eg a partner, close friendships lasting years).
Class 2 Mild impairment: Existing relationships strained. Tension and arguments with partner or close family member, loss of some friendships.
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Previously established relationships severely strained, evidenced by periods of separation or domestic violence. Spouse, relatives or community services looking after children.
Class 4 Severe impairment: Unable to form or sustain long term relationships. Pre-existing relationships ended (eg lost partner, close friends). Unable to care for dependants (eg own children, elderly parent).
Class 5 Totally impaired: Unable to function within society. Living away from populated areas, actively avoiding social contact.
Table 11.5: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - concentration, persistence and pace
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population. Able to pass a TAFE or university course within normal time frame.
Class 2 Mild impairment: Can undertake a basic retraining course, or a standard course at a slower pace. Can focus on intellectually demanding tasks for periods of up to 30 minutes, then feels fatigued or develops headache.
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Unable to read more than newspaper articles. Finds it difficult to follow complex instructions (eg operating manuals, building plans), make significant repairs to motor vehicle, type long documents, follow a pattern for making clothes, tapestry or knitting.
Class 4 Severe impairment: Can only read a few lines before losing concentration. Difficulties following simple instructions. Concentration deficits obvious even during brief concentration. Unable to live alone, or needs regular assistance from relatives or community services.
Class 5 Totally impaired: Needs constant supervision and assistance within institutional setting.
Table 11.6: Psychiatric impairment rating scale - employability
Class 1 No deficit, or minor deficit attributable to the normal variation in the general population. Able to work full time. Duties and performance are consistent with the injured worker’s education and training. The person is able to cope with the normal demands of the job.
Class 2 Mild impairment: Able to work full time but in a different environment from that of the pre-injury job. The duties require comparable skill and intellect as those of the pre-injury job. Can work in the same position, but no more than 20 hours per week (eg no longer happy to work with specific persons, or work in a specific location due to travel required).
Class 3 Moderate impairment: Cannot work at all in same position. Can perform less than 20 hours per week in a different position, which requires less skill or is qualitatively different (eg less stressful).
Class 4 Severe impairment: Cannot work more than one or two days at a time, less than 20 hours per fortnight. Pace is reduced, attendance is erratic.
Class 5 Totally impaired: Cannot work at all.
Using the PIRS to measure impairment
11.13 Rating psychiatric impairment using the PIRS is a two-step procedure:

Determine the median class score.
Calculate the aggregate score.
Determining the median class score
11.14 Each area of function described in the PIRS is given an impairment rating which ranges from Class 1 to 5. The six scores are arranged in ascending order, using the standard form. The median is then calculated by averaging the two middle scores eg:

Example A: 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5 Median Class = 3
Example B: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 Median Class = 2.5 = 3*
Example C: 1, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5 Median Class = 4
*If a score falls between two classes, it is rounded up to the next class. A median class score of 2.5 thus becomes 3.

11.15 The median class score method was chosen as it is not influenced by extremes. Each area of function is assessed separately. While impairment in one area is neither equivalent nor interchangeable with impairment in other areas, the median seems the fairest way to translate different impairments onto a linear scale.

Median class score and percentage impairment
11.16 Each median class score represents a range of impairment, as shown below:

Class 1 = 0–3%
Class 2 = 4–10%
Class 3 = 11–30%
Class 4 = 31–60%
Class 5 = 61–100%
Calculation of the aggregate score
11.17 The aggregate score is used to determine an exact percentage of impairment within a particular median class range. The six class scores are added to give the aggregate score. Use of the conversion table to arrive at percentage impairment

11.18 The aggregate score is converted to a percentage score using the conversion Table 11.7, below.

11.19 The conversion table was developed to calculate the percentage impairment based on the aggregate and median scores.

11.20 The scores within the conversion table are spread in such a way to ensure that the final percentage rating is consistent with the measurement of permanent impairment percentages for other body systems.

cat /etc/cron.d/<filename>

cat /etc/cron.daily/<filename>

Title:
News media has become more influential in people's lives. Others believe it is a negative development. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Article:
More people think the news media has become more influential in people’s lives, others think that it is a negative development. In my opinion, I partly agree with this opinion. 
On the one hand, there are many reasons that news media has become more influential in people’s live. To begin with, news can inform people about a variety of events. For example, we can access to international business and current events among different countries through the news. Apart from that, when people travel in unfamiliarly, news provides up-to-the-minute news and information. We can gain information about local weather and transportation from the news, which can make our journey more convenient. 
On the other hand, there are many reasons why some people think new media is a negative development. Firstly, news media also excessive entertainment to the audience’s click-rate. Especially about personal life scandals of celebrities, making their website incoming earn more profits. Besides, it also violates celebrities’s privacy. Secondly, the news gives a sensational title and exaggerates things to catch the reader’s eyes. As a result, people felt anxious about livelihood through this misleading news such as the global unemployment rate. Finally, certain news media platforms such as the internet and video games. It can have a negative impact early behavior development of teenagers. It often contains excessive violent content contributes to children addiction to games and violent behaviors to peers. Furthermore, excessive use of these platforms is detrimental to physical health.

This patient has fever >24 hours postpartum and uterine fundal tenderness, findings consistent with postpartum endometritis, the most common cause of postpartum fever.  Other presenting features include purulent vaginal discharge, boggy uterus, and increased vaginal bleeding.  Postpartum endometritis is a polymicrobial infection of the uterine decidua caused by ascending vaginal flora during labor, delivery, or the immediate postpartum period.  Therefore, infection is common in patients with prelabor rupture of membranes (ie, membrane rupture prior to the onset of contractions at ≥37 weeks gestation) or with protracted labor because both increase exposure of the uterine cavity to ascending bacteria.

Given the polymicrobial nature of postpartum endometritis, a broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic regimen that includes penicillin-resistant anaerobic coverage is required.  The most appropriate therapy is clindamycin plus gentamicin.  Clindamycin covers aerobic gram-positive cocci and penicillin-resistant anaerobes (eg, Bacteroides fragilis).  Gentamicin covers gram-negative (eg, Escherichia coli) and some gram-positive (eg, Staphylococcus) bacteria.  Treatment is continued until the patient is afebrile for 24 hours.

(Choice A)  Ampicillin plus gentamicin is a broad-spectrum regimen commonly used to treat intrapartum intraamniotic infection.  However, postpartum endometritis involves significantly greater anaerobic activity, and this regimen does not cover penicillin-resistant anaerobes.  However, ampicillin-sulbactam is an acceptable alternate regimen.

Intraamniotic infection is a polymicrobial infection of the placenta, amniotic fluid, membranes, or fetus; it presents with fever, maternal and/or fetal tachycardia, and uterine tenderness. Neonatal/fetal complications include in utero meconium passage, Apgar scores <6, and respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, nasal flaring, grunting).

(Choice B)  Cefoxitin plus doxycycline, which covers Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, is used to empirically treat pelvic inflammatory disease, which is also a polymicrobial infection of the upper genital tract.  However, it is not appropriate therapy in this patient because of lack of sufficient anaerobic coverage.  In addition, doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and while breastfeeding due to its potential teratogenic effects.

(Choice C)  In pregnant or breastfeeding patients, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the preferred regimen for the empiric treatment of acute cervicitis due to N gonorrhoeae and C trachomatis.  However, neither antibiotic has anaerobic coverage; therefore, this regimen would be inadequate to treat postpartum endometritis.

(Choice E)  Vancomycin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic effective only against gram-positive organisms (eg, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus).  It is indicated for the treatment of breast abscesses and for group B Streptococcus prophylaxis in penicillin-allergic patients.

grade the following on the AP Language and Composition rubric for rhetorical analysis: "With his mother's encouragement, Trevor leaves his home after high school to escape his abusive stepfather. In an effort to earn enough money for university tuition, Trevor, Sizwe, and their group start a business selling CDs to minibus drivers from a repurposed shipping container. The apartheid system has resulted in scarce job opportunities in Alexandra, particularly affecting impoverished black youth like Trevor. Although technically illegal, Trevor's actions of piracy hardly seemed "criminal" as the alternative was either working a minimum wage job or hanging out on street corners. With the help of Sizwe, the group becomes more profitable by offering credit and loans to the drivers and locals. However, despite selling CDs for two years, Trevor is no closer to saving enough for university tuition. Rather than feeling disheartened by this setback, Trevor views his lackluster achievements as mundane - it is just another day in the hood. One day, Trevor and his group are hanging out in the shipping container where they routinely tease their friend G about having a job at a nice clothing store. G enters the shipping container dressed in slippers and socks, which is not appropriate attire for work. He nonchalantly tells the group that he was fired due to accusations of theft. Trevor can't shake off the suspicion that G might have intentionally stolen, sabotaging his job to fit back in with the group. According to Trevor, the appeal of Alexandra's hood lies in its accepting environment and the avoidance of life's bigger questions.

Through interesting stylistic choices throughout the passage, the author provides important insight into the culture and society in which Trevor finds himself in Soweto. More specifically, the passage serves as an opportunity for the reader to understand the underlying realities for those, like Trevor, who lived in "the hood." It also explores implications living in the hood holds for their current lives, as well as their future prospects of escaping their current environment. Throughout the passage, the author personifies the hood, stating that “the hood has a gravitational pull," and, "the hood was strangely comforting." Using this personification the author implies that the hood is an active force in young people, like Trevor's, lives. By saying the hood has a "gravitational pull", the author insinuates that the community in which one finds themselves, similarly to gravity, is a powerful, inevitable, often inescapable force. Through this personification, the author helps the reader more fully understands the forces that perpetuate the cycle of poverty seen in Soweto, and also indirectly applauds himself for eventually escaping the commanding force that tried to drag him down. Additionally, the use of short sentences and casual dialogue when G describes the firing from his job makes the concept of a black man getting fired appear as ordinary, and almost expected. From this, the reader becomes aware of the unfortunate and unfair realities of Soweto where occurrences such as this are commonplace. This passage serves as a pertinent reminder of the profound effects a community can have on an individual and their future goals.

e-Mode Post Graduate Programme (ePGP*) in Management is a two year master degree programme (with added flexibility of completion in 3 years) offered on Interactive technology platform. The course which is imparted over more than 850 hours of classroom sessions, provides the students with leadership skills for the knowledge economy, through an innovative curriculum.

During the first year, the programme curriculum focuses on equipping the students with

Managerial decision making abilities.

Leadership capabilities.

Understanding of the functional areas of management.

Understanding of the economic and regulatory trends.

Varied analytical tools and techniques.

General management orientation.

*‘e' stands for Electronic Learning Mode (eLearning Mode)

USP of the programme
A rigorous blended learning programme in management offered by the top Indian B-School.
Award of "Master of Management Studies" (MMS) degree by IIM Ahmedabad.
IIMA is responsible for the academic policies, course design, delivery, admissions and student evaluation of ePGP. The service partner is responsible for the technology platform, infrastructure and programme management support.
Programme specifically designed for junior, mid, and senior level working professionals and entrepreneurs with all the benefits of Interactive Onsite and interactive blended Learning.

Five Classroom modules conducted in the IIMA campus at different time-slots.
Membership of IIMA Alumni association upon completion of the programme.

Valid Accounts

Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials may be used to bypass access controls placed on various resources on systems within the network and may even be used for persistent access to remote systems and externally available services, such as VPNs, Outlook Web Access, network devices, and remote desktop.[1] Compromised credentials may also grant an adversary increased privilege to specific systems or access to restricted areas of the network. Adversaries may choose not to use malware or tools in conjunction with the legitimate access those credentials provide to make it harder to detect their presence.

In some cases, adversaries may abuse inactive accounts: for example, those belonging to individuals who are no longer part of an organization. Using these accounts may allow the adversary to evade detection, as the original account user will not be present to identify any anomalous activity taking place on their account.[2]

The overlap of permissions for local, domain, and cloud accounts across a network of systems is of concern because the adversary may be able to pivot across accounts and systems to reach a high level of access (i.e., domain or enterprise administrator) to bypass access controls set within the enterprise.[3]

Mitigations
ID	Mitigation	Description
M1036	Account Use Policies	
Use conditional access policies to block logins from non-compliant devices or from outside defined organization IP ranges.[65]

M1015	Active Directory Configuration	
Disable legacy authentication, which does not support MFA, and require the use of modern authentication protocols instead.

M1013	Application Developer Guidance	
Ensure that applications do not store sensitive data or credentials insecurely. (e.g. plaintext credentials in code, published credentials in repositories, or credentials in public cloud storage).

M1027	Password Policies	
Applications and appliances that utilize default username and password should be changed immediately after the installation, and before deployment to a production environment.[66] When possible, applications that use SSH keys should be updated periodically and properly secured.

Policies should minimize (if not eliminate) reuse of passwords between different user accounts, especially employees using the same credentials for personal accounts that may not be defended by enterprise security resources.

M1026	Privileged Account Management	
Audit domain and local accounts as well as their permission levels routinely to look for situations that could allow an adversary to gain wide access by obtaining credentials of a privileged account. [3] [67] These audits should also include if default accounts have been enabled, or if new local accounts are created that have not be authorized. Follow best practices for design and administration of an enterprise network to limit privileged account use across administrative tiers. [68]

M1018	User Account Management	
Regularly audit user accounts for activity and deactivate or remove any that are no longer needed.

M1017	User Training	
Applications may send push notifications to verify a login as a form of multi-factor authentication (MFA). Train users to only accept valid push notifications and to report suspicious push notifications.

Detection
ID	Data Source	Data Component	Detects
DS0028	Logon Session	Logon Session Creation	
Monitor for newly constructed logon behavior that may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Correlate other security systems with login information (e.g., a user has an active login session but has not entered the building or does not have VPN access).

Logon Session Metadata	
Look for suspicious account behavior across systems that share accounts, either user, admin, or service accounts. Examples: one account logged into multiple systems simultaneously; multiple accounts logged into the same machine simultaneously; accounts logged in at odd times or outside of business hours. Activity may be from interactive login sessions or process ownership from accounts being used to execute binaries on a remote system as a particular account.

DS0002	User Account	User Account Authentication	
Monitor for an attempt by a user that may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

Evaluate a google company according to methods described below: Industry
Product
Culture
Benefits
Industry
Understanding how a company fits into an industry tells you a lot about the business and how they are positioned relative to other players.

How mature is the industry and how long has the company been in the space?

Are they a leader or a disruptor?

Where does the company’s offering fit into the industry relative to its competitors?

If this is a new industry relative to your existing experience, it is important to research as much as possible to understand the trends and what the future holds.

Understanding how your prospective employer fits into the industry can help prepare your cadence for your interview. Being a an exceptional candidate with stellar accomplishments only gets you so far. Showing an employer that you understand their business and how it fits into the larger picture will set you a part from other candidates.

Product
What is the product or service your prospective employer is selling? Is it something you are familiar with it or is it new to you? Either way, understanding the product or service offering can help you:

Understand the value they provide customers.
What segment of the market they are in i.e. SMB, MM, Enterprise
Future growth
No, you don’t have to love what the company is selling BUT it helps. The more you understand what they offer their customers, the better you can understand the business inside and out. Even at a more junior level, understanding the business helps you be a better candidate and in turn, a better employee regardless of the department you are interviewing for.

I understand this is more in line with how salespeople evaluate companies. However, I strongly believe it is essential for anyone applying for a job that is looking to build a successful, sustainable career.

Additionally, who else offers this product or service? How was this impacted before, during, and after COVID? This is important to understand to see if the company is trending up or not and how that affects the future of the company.

Culture
What Are Their Core Values?

Core values are important because it is not only about how a company views and values it’s employees but also how they treat customers. Do you align with their core values? Do they resonate with your own core values? Core values tell you a lot about the company and how the operate day-to-day. This is because in some cases, core values are the underpinnings of the company’s successes and failures.

Culture is nuanced and core values tell one story. What a hiring manager, team member, or website says can all vary. If they all have consistent messaging that helps. The next step is knowing whether it is authentic. A lot of companies can claim to be employee centric and then when you join the company it is a different environment than what was expected. This is the exception rather than the norm.

Benefits
Benefits can be black and white. This is where understanding the market and industry helps flesh out the laggards. How does this prospective employer stack up to other companies? Are there benefits in line with other companies you are interviewing with? Are they progressive in what they offer?

Benefits can reinforce the employee-centered culture. Based on what the hiring manager and team members tell you can let you know how the work life balance is across the organization.

I recently interviewed with a hiring manager that used the term “work-life integration” which I thought was interesting so I asked him why. He explained that with everyone working remotely that it’s difficult to maintain a balance when your work is integrated with your life. Integrating the two makes for a more successful work life which I agree.

Conclusion

Key Insights
Using the 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to Equity, Haleon fair value estimate is UK£3.56

The UK£3.53 analyst price target for HLNis comparable to our estimate of fair value.

How far off is Haleon plc (LON:HLN) from its intrinsic value? Using the most recent financial data, we'll take a look at whether the stock is fairly priced by taking the expected future cash flows and discounting them to their present value. We will take advantage of the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model for this purpose. It may sound complicated, but actually it is quite simple!

We generally believe that a company's value is the present value of all of the cash it will generate in the future. However, a DCF is just one valuation metric among many, and it is not without flaws. If you still have some burning questions about this type of valuation, take a look at the Simply Wall St analysis model.

See our latest analysis for Haleon

Is Haleon Fairly Valued?
We use what is known as a 2-stage model, which simply means we have two different periods of growth rates for the company's cash flows. Generally the first stage is higher growth, and the second stage is a lower growth phase. To begin with, we have to get estimates of the next ten years of cash flows. Where possible we use analyst estimates, but when these aren't available we extrapolate the previous free cash flow (FCF) from the last estimate or reported value. We assume companies with shrinking free cash flow will slow their rate of shrinkage, and that companies with growing free cash flow will see their growth rate slow, over this period. We do this to reflect that growth tends to slow more in the early years than it does in later years.

A DCF is all about the idea that a dollar in the future is less valuable than a dollar today, so we need to discount the sum of these future cash flows to arrive at a present value estimate

After calculating the present value of future cash flows in the initial 10-year period, we need to calculate the Terminal Value, which accounts for all future cash flows beyond the first stage. For a number of reasons a very conservative growth rate is used that cannot exceed that of a country's GDP growth. In this case we have used the 5-year average of the 10-year government bond yield (1.4%) to estimate future growth. In the same way as with the 10-year 'growth' period, we discount future cash flows to today's value, using a cost of equity of 8.3%.

Terminal Value (TV)= FCF2033 × (1 + g) ÷ (r – g) = UK£2.7b× (1 + 1.4%) ÷ (8.3%– 1.4%) = UK£40b

Present Value of Terminal Value (PVTV)= TV / (1 + r)10= UK£40b÷ ( 1 + 8.3%)10= UK£18b

The total value, or equity value, is then the sum of the present value of the future cash flows, which in this case is UK£33b. In the final step we divide the equity value by the number of shares outstanding. Relative to the current share price of UK£3.3, the company appears about fair value at a 5.9% discount to where the stock price trades currently. Remember though, that this is just an approximate valuation, and like any complex formula - garbage in, garbage out.

Important Assumptions
Now the most important inputs to a discounted cash flow are the discount rate, and of course, the actual cash flows. You don't have to agree with these inputs, I recommend redoing the calculations yourself and playing with them. The DCF also does not consider the possible cyclicality of an industry, or a company's future capital requirements, so it does not give a full picture of a company's potential performance. Given that we are looking at Haleon as potential shareholders, the cost of equity is used as the discount rate, rather than the cost of capital (or weighted average cost of capital, WACC) which accounts for debt. In this calculation we've used 8.3%, which is based on a levered beta of 1.169. Beta is a measure of a stock's volatility, compared to the market as a whole. We get our beta from the industry average beta of globally comparable companies, with an imposed limit between 0.8 and 2.0, which is a reasonable range for a stable business.

Annual earnings are forecast to grow slower than the British market.

Valuation is only one side of the coin in terms of building your investment thesis, and it is only one of many factors that you need to assess for a company. The DCF model is not a perfect stock valuation tool. Preferably you'd apply different cases and assumptions and see how they would impact the company's valuation. Make this into one logical personal statement that explains why I want to study International Relations in University
International relations has a tremendous impact on global affairs, and this characteristic entices me to delve deeper into its study. Understanding the dynamics of international relations allows me to comprehend how interactions between nations shape world politics, economics, and social dynamics. This knowledge empowers me to comprehend major global events, such as conflicts, alliances, or economic partnerships, and their implications for different countries and regions. By studying international relations, I can become an active participant in shaping the global order, contributing to peacebuilding, conflict resolution, and cooperation between states.

Furthermore, studying international relations cultivates critical thinking and analytical skills, another aspect that attracts me to this field. Analyzing documents, treaties, policies, and geopolitical strategies requires a thorough examination of diverse perspectives and evidence-based reasoning. International relations necessitates the ability to evaluate and interpret complex information, assess its reliability, and draw informed conclusions. These skills are invaluable not only in academia but also in a wide range of career paths, including diplomacy, politics, journalism, international organizations, and consulting, among others.
In addition, the interdisciplinary nature of international relations is a key factor that ignites my interest in studying it. This field draws knowledge from various disciplines such as politics, economics, sociology, history, law, and even psychology. This interdisciplinary approach enables me to develop a holistic understanding of global issues, as it recognizes the complex web of factors that influence the dynamics between countries. By analyzing international relations through a multifaceted lens, I can gain profound insights into the underlying causes, consequences, and possible solutions to global challenges.
Ever since my childhood, I have been captivated by history and diplomacy. One pivotal moment that sparked my interest in studying International Relations was during my fifth-grade Chinese history class. As we delved into the fascinating era of the Three Kingdoms Period, I came across the character of Sima Yi, renowned for his exceptional diplomatic skills. Sima Yi’s ability to navigate complex political landscapes and forge alliances left a lasting impression on me. I was drawn to the idea of bridging gaps between nations through effective diplomacy. This early encounter planted the seeds of curiosity and ambition in my young mind 

As I entered middle school, my exposure to the world outside of China expanded exponentially. My father’s business engagements with partners from various countries, including Portugal, Spain, the USA, UK, Thailand, Singapore, and Vietnam, afforded me the opportunity to meet people from different cultures. One encounter with a Jewish businessman shed light on the nuances of cultural differences. I discovered that he carried 8 liters of a specific brand of milk when traveling to China because it was the only type he would consume. This experience made me realize how diverse perspectives and practices can exist even within seemingly everyday aspects of life. It ignited, within me, a thirst to explore these differences on a larger scale and understand the intricacies of global cultures 

During high school, my desire to comprehend global dynamics led me to participate in an exchange program in Germany. It was a transformative experience that challenged the narratives I had been exposed to in China. Software Engineering-MASc Program overview
The Master of Applied Science in Software Engineering (MASc.SE) is a course-based master’s program intended for students with a computer science or computer engineering background who wish to upgrade their background to specialize in software engineering. The MASc.SE is a four-term, course-based master’s program offered jointly by the Faculty of Engineering and Applied Science and the Faculty of Science. Graduates of the program will have knowledge and understanding of the core areas and methods in software engineering and will be ready to work in positions of software development, computer systems architecture and design, and distributed services. The program distinguishes itself from existing course options in computer science and computer engineering with its increased focus on software engineering and related topics and a decreased emphasis on other areas, such as hardware, digital design and communications. 

Seven core courses (3 credit hours each)
ENGI 9818 Software Fundamentals
ENGI 9867 Advanced Computing Concepts for Engineering
ENGI 9874 Software Design and Specification
ENGI 9839 Software Verification and Validation
ENGI 9837† Software Engineering Capstone
COMP 6901 Applied Algorithms
COMP 6905 Software Engineering

† Normally ENGI 9837 will be taken in the final term

Three elective courses selected from the following courses or with the program chair’s approval

ENGI 9807 Computer Security or COMP 6916 Security and Privacy
ENGI 9838 Software Engineering Practice
ENGI 9861 High-performance Computer Architecture or COMP 6904 Advanced Computer Architecture
ENGI 9869 Advanced Concurrent Programming or COMP 6903Concurrent Computing
ENGI 9872 Digital Communications
ENGI 9875 Embedded and Real-time Systems Design or COMP 6925 Advanced Operating Systems
ENGI 9876 Advanced Data Networks
ENGI 9877 Cryptography

Based on the report given, it appears that the individual has several knee issues, including a complex medial meniscal tear, a fracture in the subchondral bone of the medial tibial plateau, severe damage to the cartilage between the patella (kneecap) and femur (thigh bone), inflammation of the pes anserinus bursa (a fluid-filled sac near the inner side of the knee), and mucoid degeneration of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

1. Complex medial meniscal tear: This refers to a tear in the meniscus, which is a cartilage structure that provides cushioning and stability to the knee joint. A complex tear implies that the tear extends into multiple areas or is of a more severe nature.

2. Subchondral fracture of the medial tibial plateau: This means there is a fracture in the bone just below the cartilage found on the inner part of the upper surface of the tibia (shinbone). This is the area where the femur rests, and a fracture here can affect the stability and function of the knee joint.

3. Severe patellofemoral chondral pathology: This indicates significant damage to the cartilage between the patella (kneecap) and the femur (thigh bone). This damage can result in pain, reduced range of motion, and decreased function of the knee joint.

4. Pes anserinus bursitis: Pes anserinus bursitis refers to inflammation of the pes anserinus bursa, a small fluid-filled sac located near the inner side of the knee. This condition is typically associated with overuse or injury and can cause pain and swelling in the knee.

5. Mucoid degeneration of ACL: Mucoid degeneration refers to the breakdown and abnormal thickening of the fibers within a structure. In this case, it is the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in the knee that is affected. This degeneration can weaken the ligament, leading to instability and increased risk of further injury.

Overall, this report suggests that the individual has multiple knee problems, including various tears, fractures, cartilage damage, and inflammation. It is important for them to seek appropriate medical treatment to address these issues and manage the symptoms.

Summarise this and whether it is saying interest rates are likely to increase? "The RBA’s Statement on Monetary Policy elaborates on the reasoning behind this week’s decision to raise the cash rate. Underlying inflation has not declined as fast as the RBA expected a year ago or three months ago. The inflation forecasts have been revised up and most of the risks are to the upside, including domestic services inflation, rising medium-term inflation expectations and weak productivity boosting growth in effective labour costs. The RBA highlighted their concerns about the higher inflation outlook by adding a graph showing both current and August forecasts for trimmed mean inflation in addition to the usual forecast-with-uncertainty-bands graph.

 

The RBA has been surprised by the resilience of domestic demand, especially outside the household sector; this is another factor that will tend to lift inflation. Near-term GDP growth is now expected to be stronger, with some of the resilience of business investment seen in the first half of 2023 carrying over into the second half. Our own forecasts embed a view that much of this first-half strength in equipment spending was a pull-forward to take advantage of tax breaks, which will not be repeated in the second half. Likewise, some of the strength was a catch-up as supply chain disruptions dissipated, a process that will come to an end at some point. On the other hand, more investment is needed to restore the ratio of capital to labour to earlier trends, and so support the needed improvement in productivity.

 

As flagged in the Governor’s decision statement, the unemployment rate profile has also been revised down. It might be that the RBA is expecting more of the softening in labour market conditions to come through underemployment than previously thought. The labour market has clearly turned, though it remains tight; the SMP points to a range of indicators in support of this assessment, including youth and medium-term unemployment, as well as underemployment.

 

These upside revisions to the forecast have occurred despite a roughly ¼ percentage point higher assumed profile for the cash rate, based on market pricing and private sector forecasts. The peak is around 4½%, which does not imply that further increases after November’s are baked in.

 

Central to these changes is the upward revision to assumed population growth. Both GDP growth and employment growth are about ½ percentage point higher in the forecast for 2024 than in the RBA’s August forecasts. Because the extra population adds to both supply and demand, the effect on unemployment and (non-housing) inflation is marginal at best. There is, however, a significant effect on the housing market. The SMP text calls out the strong growth in rents, rising housing prices and increases in average household size in the major cities as being connected to this dynamic.

 

Despite the forecast upgrades, GDP growth is expected to remain slow. The household sector is being squeezed by the higher cost of living, rising tax take and, increasingly, the effect of higher interest rates. The consumption forecasts for 2024 were revised down noticeably (­–0.3%points), with no growth payback in 2025. Given the higher population assumption, this is a material downgrade on a per person basis. It also aligns with what we are seeing in our Card Tracker data (see Westpac Senior Economist Matt Hassan’s report earlier today).

 

The RBA notes that falling real household incomes are driving the weakness in consumer spending. The Bank’s real household disposable income forecast for year to June quarter 2024 has been revised down 1½ percentage points to –1.1%. Such is the weakness in the income forecasts that even the current weak consumption forecasts can only be sustained with a near-zero household saving ratio in the first half of 2024.

 

It is hard to conceive how such an extended period of declining real incomes – even worse in per household terms – can coexist with a still-tight labour market. It is also a little hard to square the still-tight labour market and cost of living squeeze with the downward revision to the forecast path for wages growth and (in 2024) average earnings. While the forecast bounce-back in household incomes is also a bit sharper, the experience of the Australian household sector will stand in contrast to its counterparts overseas.

 

Most of the other changes speak to increasing concerns that inflation will not come down as quickly as the Board intends. The language around weak productivity growth continues to highlight inflation risks. The SMP overview states, “the forecasts assume that productivity growth will pick up, which will be needed for labour cost growth to be consistent with the inflation target”. In August, the assumption was that productivity growth would return to pre-pandemic trends. The SMP text calls this out as being a particular issue for services inflation, which embeds a larger share of labour costs than do goods prices. Another important change in language in the SMP overview is the recognition that some measures of medium-term inflation expectations have risen a little lately.

 

Because services inflation has been so sticky, the RBA is also sceptical that disinflation abroad is assured. It believes that ‘[t]he risk that inflation takes even longer to return to target has increased.’ On the other hand, the risks to global growth were held to be tilted to the downside. We agree, but there is a tension in how these risks sit together.

 

The Board considered both the case to hold and the case to increase rates at the November meeting. As we expected, the case to raise rates was stronger. The chance that the Board will need to do more, presumably in February, is also rising. The refreshed forecasts embed very little margin for upside surprises on inflation.  "
