A computer
 

Read the following guidelines carefully before starting the job. 

Guidelines for transcription
 

Whatever is pronounced by the speaker must be transcribed, including elements that are not strictly verbal, such as:  

False starts 
Hesitations/Fillers 
Repetitions 
Interjections (exclamations) 
Truncations or interruptions 
Illogical and/or ungrammatical content 
To guide you through this, the instructions have been organized into two sections: 

1. Quality & Discourse tags 

2. Transcription rules  

Read them both carefully. 

1. Quality & Discourse tags 
Quality tags 
Cut off
if the recording begins and/or ends abruptly, cutting off a word at the beginning and/or end of the file, insert the tag Cut_off. Use this tag only when you are 100% sure, if in doubt, do not use it. Do make the necessary corrections to the transcription.

Note
Do NOT use this tag if the speaker stutters (in this case, refer to the relevant point in the Transcription rules section below).  
Audio example:

 Transcription: Speaker 1 yes I was thinking of going to the supermar  Cut_off

 

If the whole recording does not include verbal speech, use the tag Empty.
Note
Background noises can be present in an empty audio fragment, and you do not need to transcribe or tag those, the focus is on speech from the main speaker. 

Audio example:

 Transcription: Empty  

Discourse tags 


Unintelligible
Words or parts of speech that are not understandable (due to overlaps, garbled speech, interfering conversation in the background, acoustic issues, etc.) should be flagged in the transcription by entering the Unintelligible tag at the exact point in the recording where they occur.  

 

Audio example:

 Transcription: Speaker 1 yes so I Unintelligible "Carla" will do it yes



Hesitation
If the speaker hesitates or affirms/agrees by emitting undefined sounds such as fillers (e.g. um, uh, ah, oh, ahah, etc.), use the Hesitation/Filler  tag. Each hesitation or affirmation must be tagged individually. If the speaker utters 2 or 3 hesitations/affirmations in a row, you must add the equivalent amount of tags to the transcription.  
Note
Only use this tag to flag isolated fillers. If the speaker turns a word into a filler, do not enter this tag. Just transcribe the word as you understand it.  

Audio examples:

Hesitation

Transcription: Speaker 1 Hesitation/Filler well I don't know Hesitation/Filler I would have to check that with my sister

 

Affirmation

Transcription: Speaker 1 Hesitation/Filler  of course I will send you the link to that recipe so you can try it



Speaker tag
Please use the speaker identification tags Speaker 1, Speaker 2, Speaker 3, Speaker 4, Speaker 5 whenever a speaker is producing speech. This applies for all of the transcriptions that contain speech expect for the cases where the audio file is empty. The transcription should begin with the relevant speaker tag, followed by the spoken content. If there is a switch to another speaker, use the corresponding speaker tag and continue transcribing the speech for that speaker. Reuse the tags as needed, following the order of speakers in the audio file, up to a maximum of five speakers.

Audio examples:

Transcription: Speaker 1 that's hysterical Speaker 2 you know what I mean like I was like  Speaker 1 yeah Speaker 2 oh what a weird way to call it I mean sure but why Non-speech: laughter Speaker 1 that's crazy that






Overlapping Speech
Please use the overlapping speech tag to indicate overlapping speech in the transcription. Apply this tag whenever two or more speakers are speaking simultaneously, and transcribe all content produced by each speaker during the overlap.

Audio examples:


Transcription: Speaker 1 crashed into it spewing Overlapping Speech Speaker 2  thirty seconds remaining Speaker 1 enormous volumes of planetary debris into space that eventually accumulated into becoming the moon



Non-Speech tagging:

Non-speech: music - Please use non-speech music to tag any music sounds or melodies in the transcription. This tag is specifically for instances where music is present, including cases where there are lyrics, but the lyrics should not be transcribed.



Non-speech: applause - Please use the non-speech applause tag to flag instances of applause in the transcription, designating moments where applause is present in the audio file as non-speech.



Non-speech: laughter - Please use the non-speech laughter tag to mark instances of laughter in the transcription, indicating moments where someone is laughing in the audio file as non-speech.



Non-speech: screaming - Please use non-speech screaming tag to mark instances of screaming in the transcription, indicating moments where someone is screaming in the audio file as non-speech.



Non-speech: crying/sobbing - Please use non-speech crying/sobbing tag to mark instances of crying or sobbing in the transcription, specifying moments where someone is crying or sobbing in the audio file as non-speech.



Non-speech: other - Please use non-speech other tag to mark any noises or sounds that do not belong to verbal speech in the transcription. This includes but is not limited to coughing, sneezing, hiccupping, breathing loudly, audio glitches, background noises (such as objects falling, chimes, people talking in the background, TV, music, dogs barking, noise from appliances, etc.).


Note
If the noise/sound is continuous, just tag it once where it first occurs in the recording. 
Audio examples:

Transcription: Speaker 1 I wanted to go actually to the cinema and see a movie Non-speech: other but Hesitation/Filler it's just not possible with the Non-speech:other with the confinement yeah so I have to stay home

2. Transcription Rules 




NUMBERS AND SYMBOLS must be transcribed as words, in the way they are articulated by the speaker in the audio recording.
Examples:
in 1997 = in nineteen ninety-seven 
Oakland 94612 = "Oakland" nine four six one two   
50 $ = fifty dollars 
Note
Numbers that are part of products or brands names (for instance, iPhone 7) must be transcribed using digits:

iPhone 7 = "iPhone 7"
Audi R8 = "Audi R. 8"
Windows 10 = "Windows 10"
Audio examples:

 Transcription: Speaker 1 yes I paid fifty-five dollars for this table

 

 Transcription: Speaker 1 the code is thirteen twenty-one yes one three two one 

 

To report STUTTERING and/or WORDS TRUNCATION, enter a hyphen followed by a blank space precisely where the stuttering or truncation takes place:  
stuttering: l- la- late 
truncation: perf- no sorry 
Audio example:

Transcription: Speaker 1 well I just think this looks fan- this looks fantastic it's amazing

Note
In case of words repetition, there is no need to add the hyphen, the word simply needs to be written as many times as it is said.

repetition: I can can can do that
 

Words must be transcribed following the SPELLING RULES  of English.
don’t NOT  dont  
acknowledge  NOT  acknowlege  
independent  NOT  independant  
they should have shown NOT  they should of shown
shorty NOT shawty 
Note
Do NOT use commas, question or exclamation marks, semicolons, colons, or periods:

can you kindly provide me with your phone number first name surname and date of birth

NOT: can you kindly provide me with your phone number, first name, surname, and date of birth?

Please remember to accurately transcribe ungrammatical content and colloquialisms as well:  

if you would have ask me I could have helped you 
I was gonna ask you to join 
I dunno I gotta go  
When in doubt, please refer to a dictionary to make sure of the correct spelling.
Lack of capital letters at the beginning of transcription is not an error. Elsewhere, capital letters should only occur where required by rule (for example, proper names, place names, etc.). Please, proceed to correct them when they unexpectedly occur in other contexts.
 

PROPER NAMES (that is, first and last names), place names, addresses, brands, weekdays, months, products should be enclosed between quotation marks and spelled according to their official spelling. Please, capitalize the first letter and make sure to use double quotes " " and NOT « » or single quotes '' ''. Products names should be written as they are officially given. 
Examples
"Jack Johnson" said that "Susan" stopped in "Miami"
“Mark” bought a new “iPhone” yesterday
"Rachel" admires "Wal-Mart's" supply chain
the nearest branch is at forty-one “Paterson Street”
it is cold in "January"

Quotation marks should be used to transcribe proper names and brands included in email addresses and URLs as well.

<PRESIDIO_ANONYMIZED_EMAIL_ADDRESS> = "Sherri” dot “Clark" at "Gmail" dot com
www.google.com = W. W. W. dot “Google” dot com
 

LETTERS PRONOUNCED IN ISOLATION, for example, in the spelling of a word, should be transcribed using capital letters followed by a period and a blank space after each letter and enclosed between quotation marks when the letters make up a proper name. Please make sure to use double quotes " " and NOT « » or single quotes '' ''. 
Examples
my name is "Diana" "D. I. A. N. A. " 
no not B. it’s P. as in "Paris"  
www.google.com = W. W. W. dot "Google" dot com  
Audio example:

 Transcription: Speaker 1 my name is "Diana" "D. I. A. N. A. "  


ACRONYMS pronounced as REAL WORDS should be transcribed in capital letters without dots or spaces.
Examples
"NASA" 
"UNESCO"  
Note
Acronyms pronounced as sets of letters (that is, initalisms) should be transcribed as explained in the previous point: LETTERS PRONOUNCED IN ISOLATION. For example:
T. V.
A. T. M. 
Note
Acronyms can be proper nouns, in that case, please make sure to apply both the rules for acronyms as well as the rules for proper nouns:
"NASA" 
"N. S. A. "
 

ABBREVIATIONS are NOT accepted. Please, write the whole word instead: 
Examples
doctor "Jones" NOT Dr. "Jones" 
missus "Lippman"  NOT Mrs. "Lippman"

It provides a no-cost, easy-to-use platform that supports the complete machine learning development lifecycle, allowing users to build, train, and deploy machine learning models.

Here are some key aspects of Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab:

1. No Cost: Studio Lab is free, making it accessible to individuals and organizations that want to experiment with or start learning about machine learning without incurring cloud costs.

2. Ease of Use: It offers a web-based integrated development environment (IDE) based on Jupyter Lab, which is familiar to many data scientists and researchers. This environment supports Python and comes pre-installed with many popular data science and machine learning libraries, such as Pandas, NumPy, TensorFlow, PyTorch, and SciKit-Learn.

3. Compute Resources: Users get access to certain compute resources for running notebooks and training models. While free, these resources are subject to usage limits to ensure fair access for all users.

4. Managed Jupyter Notebooks: The service manages Jupyter notebooks, including their setup, configurations, and dependencies, which reduces the setup time for users and allows them to focus more on their experiments and models.

5. Collaboration: SageMaker Studio Lab allows users to share their projects and collaborate with others, which is beneficial for educational purposes and team projects.

6. Seamless Transition to AWS: For projects that outgrow the capabilities of the free tier or require more advanced features, users can easily move their projects to AWS and leverage the full suite of Amazon SageMaker services for scaling their machine learning models and applications.

7. Education and Learning: It is also designed as a learning platform, offering access to tutorials and examples that cover various aspects of machine learning, from the basics to more advanced topics.

Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab is part of Amazon’s broader SageMaker suite, which provides more comprehensive and scalable services for machine learning and AI project development. Studio Lab is an excellent starting point for individuals and organizations new to machine learning or those looking to prototype models without significant investment.
But how it’s made free?
Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab is made free to users as part of Amazon Web Services’ broader strategy to encourage the adoption of their cloud platform and machine learning technologies. While the service itself does not incur direct costs to users for accessing its basic features and resources, there are several strategic reasons and mechanisms behind its free offering:

1. Fostering Adoption: By providing free access to SageMaker Studio Lab, AWS aims to lower the barrier to entry for learning and experimenting with machine learning and artificial intelligence. This democratization of access not only helps in building a larger community of ML practitioners but also increases the likelihood that these individuals and organizations will use AWS’s paid services as their needs grow.

2. Educational Support: AWS is investing in the education of future developers, data scientists, and ML engineers by providing them with tools to learn and experiment at no cost. Educated users are more likely to become future customers or recommend AWS services within their organizations.

3. Resource Limits: While Studio Lab is free, it comes with certain limitations on compute resources and usage. These limitations help AWS manage cost while still providing value to users. For projects that require more resources or advanced features, users are encouraged to transition to the more comprehensive, paid version of SageMaker or other AWS services.

4. Cost of Acquisition: Offering free services like SageMaker Studio Lab can be seen as a customer acquisition cost. Acquiring a user through free services and eventually converting them into a paying customer for other services can be more cost-effective than traditional marketing and sales efforts.

5. Upsell and Cross-Sell Opportunities: Engaging users with a free service opens up opportunities for AWS to upsell more advanced features and cross-sell other services within its ecosystem. As users’ projects and needs grow, they might need more storage, compute power, or specific AWS features not covered under the free tier of Studio Lab.

6. Community Building and Feedback: A large base of users experimenting with and learning through SageMaker Studio Lab contributes to the machine learning and AI community. It also provides AWS with valuable feedback and usage patterns, helping them improve their platform and develop new features that address users’ needs.

By offering SageMaker Studio Lab for free, Amazon benefits from creating a large community of users who are familiar with AWS technologies, potentially leading to future revenue as these users’ needs evolve and require the capabilities of AWS’s paid services.

PyTorch Lightning aims to abstract and automate much of the routine work involved in machine learning projects, allowing researchers and developers to focus more on their experiments instead of boilerplate code.

Lightning AI provides several key features and benefits that cater to machine learning practitioners and researchers:

1. Simplification: It simplifies the process of building, training, and deploying machine learning models by handling much of the underlying complexity. This includes automating repetitive tasks such as running experiments in parallel, managing datasets, and tracking experiments.

2. Scalability: The platform allows users to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs and even across clusters of machines. This scalability is vital for training complex models on large datasets.

3. Reproducibility: Lightning AI emphasizes reproducibility in machine learning experiments. It provides tools and best practices to help ensure that experiments can be repeated and results can be verified by others.

4. Collaboration: The platform supports team collaboration, making it easier for groups of researchers and developers to work together on machine learning projects. This includes sharing experiments, results, and models in a centralized manner.

5. Integration: Lightning AI integrates with popular tools and platforms used in the machine learning ecosystem, such as Weights & Biases for experiment tracking and GitHub for version control, enhancing its utility and flexibility.

6. Community and Resources: Being built around PyTorch Lightning, it benefits from a strong community of developers and researchers. Users have access to a wealth of tutorials, documentation, and pre-built models to accelerate their projects.

Overall, Lightning AI represents a part of the broader trend towards democratizing AI development, providing high-level tools that abstract away complexity and make machine learning more accessible to a wider range of users.

To calculate how long you can sustain a free plan where you give $15 per user per month to 100,000 users with an investment of $54 million, you can follow these steps:

1. First, calculate the total monthly cost of the free plan by multiplying the amount given per user by the total number of users:
[
\text{Monthly Cost} = \text{Amount per User} \times \text{Number of Users}
]
[
\text{Monthly Cost} = $15 \times 100,000 = $1,500,000
]

2. Then, divide the total investment by the monthly cost to find out how many months you can sustain the plan:
[
\text{Duration in Months} = \frac{\text{Total Investment}}{\text{Monthly Cost}}
]
[
\text{Duration in Months} = \frac{$54,000,000}{$1,500,000} = 36
]

So, with an investment of $54 million, you can sustain a free plan that gives $15 to each of 100,000 users per month for 36 months, or equivalently, 3 years.
What if only allocate 10 million dollars for free plan
If you allocate $10 million specifically for the free plan, where you give $15 per user per month to 100,000 users, here’s how you would calculate the duration for which you can sustain this plan:

]

2. Divide the allocated budget for the free plan by the monthly cost to determine how many months you can maintain the plan:
[
\text{Duration in Months} = \frac{\text{Allocated Budget}}{\text{Monthly Cost}} = \frac{$10,000,000}{$1,500,000} \approx 6.67
]

Therefore, with a $10 million allocation for the free plan, you could sustain the plan for approximately 6.67 months. 1. Approved Product Notes: A document outlining the details, features, and rules of a financial product that has been approved for offering to customers.

2. Policy Document: Contains the rules and guidelines of how a specific process or product works. It’s the rule book for a company’s offerings or procedures.

3. Pricing Matrix: A chart or document that shows the pricing structure for a company’s products or services, including any discounts or special rates.

4. SOP (Standard Operating Procedure): A set of step-by-step instructions compiled by an organization to help workers carry out routine operations.

5. Manual: A detailed handbook or guide explaining how something works or how to do something, often for training purposes.

6. Addendum: An addition or supplement to a document, often containing changes, updates, or extra information that was not included in the original.

7. Extract of FICO Rules and Deviations in SFDC System: A summary of the financial (credit score-related) rules and any exceptions to these rules that are programmed into the Salesforce (SFDC) system.

8. UAT Signoff: Sign-off at the end of User Acceptance Testing, confirming that a software or system meets requirements and is ready for deployment.

9. Latest Business Review Document (BRD): A document that captures the business requirements for a project or system, most recently updated.

10. Credit Authority Matrix / CAD Limit: A guideline outlining who has the authority to approve credit and up to what limit.

11. Risk Register: A document listing all identified risks to a project or business, along with impact assessment and mitigation plans.

12. Stamp Duty Master in SFDC: A record in Salesforce detailing the stamp duty fees applicable for various transactions.

13. List of Fraud Cases: A document listing instances of fraud identified within the organization or related to its products/services.

14. PDD MIS (Post Disbursement Documents Management Information System): A system or report tracking the collection and management of documents after a loan or credit has been disbursed.

15. Pricing Matrix and Deviation Matrix: Documents that outline the standard pricing and any deviations (special cases) from those prices.

16. Risk-Based Pricing Manual: Guidelines on setting prices for loans or services based on the risk profile of the customer.

17. List of Product Codes and Schemes: A comprehensive list of the codes and details for each product or scheme the company offers, stating which are currently active or inactive.

18. Portfolio MIS (Management Information System): Reports and systems used to manage and review the financial portfolio of a business, including loans, investments, etc.

19. Collateral Register: A record of all assets that have been pledged as security (collateral) for loans or obligations.

20. Schedule of Charges: A detailed list of all fees and charges that a company applies to its services or products.

21. Disbursement MIS: Reports on the funds that have been paid out (disbursed) for loans or other financial products.

22. Rejection Dump: A report listing all applications or requests that have been rejected, including reasons and details of any communications sent.

23. Demand Draft Issuance including Cancellation: The process and records of issuing bank drafts for payments and their cancellation if necessary.

24. MIS on RCU Screening: Reports detailing the cases that have been screened or sampled by the Risk Control Unit (RCU) and their outcomes.

25. Empanelled Agencies List: A list of external agencies approved to conduct valuation, legal, technical due diligence, or other services for the company.

26. Insurance Policy Issuance Tracker: Records tracking the issuance of insurance policies, including details of claims if applicable.

27. CERSAI MIS: Reports on transactions (creation, modification, pending, removed) recorded with the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI).

28. Monthwise Incentive Paid MIS: Reports detailing the incentives paid out to employees or partners, typically on a monthly basis, including calculations and criteria.

(REs) since 2003, REs are required to release all movable / immovable property
documents upon receiving full repayment and closure of loan account. However, it has
been observed that the REs follow divergent practices in release of such movable /
immovable property documents leading to customer grievances and disputes. To address
the issues faced by the borrowers and towards promoting responsible lending conduct
among the REs, the following Directions are being issued:
Release of Movable / Immovable Property Documents
2. The REs shall release all the original movable / immovable property documents and
remove charges registered with any registry within a period of 30 days after full
repayment/ settlement of the loan account.
3. The borrower shall be given the option of collecting the original movable / immovable
property documents either from the banking outlet / branch where the loan account was
serviced or any other office of the RE where the documents are available, as per her / his
preference.
1 As defined in Annex to the Circular on ‘XBRL Returns – Harmonization of Banking Statistics’ dated January

2
4. The timeline and place of return of original movable / immovable property documents
will be mentioned in the loan sanction letters issued on or after the effective date.
5. In order to address the contingent event of demise of the sole borrower or joint
borrowers, the REs shall have a well laid out procedure for return of original movable /
immovable property documents to the legal heirs. Such procedure shall be displayed on
the website of the REs along with other similar policies and procedures for customer
information.
Compensation for delay in release of Movable / Immovable Property Documents
6. In case of delay in releasing of original movable / immovable property documents or
failing to file charge satisfaction form with relevant registry beyond 30 days after full
repayment/ settlement of loan, the RE shall communicate to the borrower reasons for
such delay. In case where the delay is attributable to the RE, it shall compensate the
borrower at the rate of ₹5,000/- for each day of delay.
7. In case of loss/damage to original movable / immovable property documents, either in
part or in full, the REs shall assist the borrower in obtaining duplicate/certified copies of
the movable / immovable property documents and shall bear the associated costs, in
addition to paying compensation as indicated at paragraph 6 above. However, in such
cases, an additional time of 30 days will be available to the REs to complete this
procedure and the delayed period penalty will be calculated thereafter (i.e., after a total
period of 60 days).
8. The compensation provided under these directions shall be without prejudice to the
rights of a borrower to get any other compensation as per any applicable law.
Applicability
9. These Directions shall be applicable to all cases where release of original movable /
immovable property documents falls due on or after December 1, 2023.
10. The above Directions are issued under sections 21, 35A and 56 of the Banking
Regulation Act, 1949, sections 45JA and 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934,

We are looking for artistic research contributions that investigate speculative approaches to sound synthesis, computation, and music technology. These contributions should explore aesthetic positions that offer alternative perspectives to standardized ways of thinking and creating. Speculation as an artistic practice is understood as a situated oscillation between experience and imagination, bringing forth new forms of knowledge and opening up to new kinds of aesthetic thinking.
At the core of this speculative oscillation is the question of how computational technologies’ generative potential can be made aesthetically experienceable and productive. The symposium aims to unite speculative approaches that make computational processes perceptible and address the tension between contingency and control in artistic practice. What are the implications of considering sound synthesis as a form of composition and musical composition as a form of sound synthesis? What are the specific potentials of sound as a trace of computation and as a perceptual object in this constellation of technology and aesthetics?
~~~
Here my abstract:
~~~
This composition pioneers a speculative approach to sound synthesis by employing tetrahedral geometry within spherical loudspeakers arrays, alongside a distinctive tuning process performed by the interpreter. This process involves identifying frequencies within a defined range that enhance spatial auditory qualities, through modalities like zeroth and first order Ambisonics propagation, thereby tailoring the performance to the unique acoustics of the space. Utilizing a custom-developed granular synthesis technique, realized through a dedicated C++ software, the work invites a recalibration of standard sound synthesis paradigms by intertwining the precise geometry of loudspeakers with the acoustic characteristics of performance spaces. Crucially, the inclusion of a pre-performance, listening-based tuning by the interpreter to align with the room’s acoustical properties, presents a ‘what if’ scenario that reimagines the role of instrumentalists in acousmatic music as active listeners and responders to the environment. Instead of delivering a fixed-media piece, this approach allows for a live, adaptive interplay between the composition, technology, and the unique spatial qualities of each performance environment. The resulting work not only challenges traditional auditory experiences but also opens new avenues for artistic exploration in the integration of sound synthesis, spatial audio, and live performance within music technology.
~~~
Here my detailed overview of the project:
~~~
1. Detailed Overview of the Project: the submission is related to introduce the reader to an acousmatic music composition I wrote called “Campi Instabili”, where I used an outer-radiating spherical loudspeakers array, called S.T.One, that is based on tetrahedral geometry. The tetrahedron is 3-simplex, such that is the simplest approximation to the sphere. This allows to explore low-order Ambisonics usage in an outer-radiating spherical loudspeakers array. Indeed, it is possible to have a zeroth order Ambisonics reproduction while reproducing the same sound on the four loudspeakers at the same time. Also, it is possible to have a first order Ambisonics reproduction. Moreover, the tetrahedron is symmetric, favoring geometrical consideration and reasoning. Finally, loudspeakers are well-distanced, such that the cross-talk cancellation and effect are minimized. In particular, in this piece I developed a custom granular synthesis, done directly in conjunction with the spherical loudspeakers array itself. Indeed, developing such technique allows me to write directly for this hardware, making it custom and allowing patterns directly thought for the such a combination of loudspeakers. Indeed, a more traditional approach is based on reason in Ambisonics order, and to compose with them. On the contrary, traditional speaker arrays, if based on Ambisonics paradigm, are in a inner perspective, i.e., the listener is in the center of the focus. Outer-radiating paradigm is based on setting the loudspeaker on the center, like it should happen in a traditional concert with an instrumentalist. Moreover, this approach binds the instrument, in this case the outer-radiating loudspeakers array, to the space and its acoustics, while a traditional approach, like an Ambisonics dome, tends to minimize the role of the room, while recreating an virtual acoustical environment. Moreover, often the space where High-Order Ambisonics loudspeakers arrays are located can be acoustically treated, to further minimize the effect of the acoustical space. On the contrary, such an approach tends to bind the loudspeaker to the room's acoustics. This approach provides a more robust foundation on focusing on relationship between loudspeakers, and not to polar pattern. The granular synthesis is based only on synthetic material, in particular on sinusoidal wave. This allows to consider relationship between loudspeakers directly as difference in phases between sinosoidal waves, and avoiding to create first order Ambisonics while reproducing the sound in two loudspeakers countephase respect the other two. Indeed, the counterphase is giving as a temporal consequence giving by a difference in phase between a wave and another one, or differently stated between its delayed version. The piece explores a pre-performance in which using a listening-based tuning phase the interpreter can set the proper frequencies the piece will use. This is done by listening how the room responses to some low-order propagation of sound, while propagating some sinousoidal tone in zeroth order Ambisonics and first order Ambisonics. During the composition phase, I noted that a little variation in frequency can have huge different in acoustic response, mainly related to creation of standing waves and reverberation. Indeed, the piece is composed mainly of sinusoidal synthetic waves, such that a fine tune is important to find if a specific frequency improves the general perception of the space, like improving the clarity in some granular passages, or improving sound localization by sounds that are concentrated in a given part of the room due to the standing waves. Indeed, the interpreter has to listen particular except of the piece that are based on these specifics, to clear the compositional underpinnings. Moreover, even the position of the spherical loudspekears array has to be find by the interpreter, while I provided some guidance in the score. Actually, the decision-making process is guided by listening some piece's passages at different frequencies in a given range, to maximize the dialogue the piece tries to have between the loudspeakers and the space. Criteria are listening-based, such that granular passages that acts as "pizzicato" have to be clearly intelligible, while a section at the end of the piece, where granular synthesis is used a modulation to create complex spectra, has to resonate such to create strong localized reverbs, due to the standing waves. All the piece’s software has been written by me in C++, using only a well-known library for handling the file audio creation (the library is libsndfile). The C++ source code includes both the score and the granular synthesis. At the beginning of the source code, the interpreter finds the settings to be adjusted during the tuning phase. After the build process, done using a provided Makefile, the program renders directly the wav file. The piece tries to create an interaction with the room itself, exploring the spatial perception of the room and answering to the question "what if the loudspeakers is a traditional instrumentalist. This approach provides an active and central role to the loudspeaker and to interpreter, that is responsible for a correct tuning phase. The project expand the traditional boundaries of acousmatic music because it tries to focus on specific relationship between a loudspeaker that can propagate 3D sound, the room, and compositional strategies that tend to bind these aspects. Indeed, music technologies, i.e., custom-developed granular synthesis, has been written specifically to maximize these relationships, while providing a vivid space perception. The piece aims to make experiential my compositional interest in space, intended as the place where a continuity between all the structure's addends of the piece in an ecosystemic view exist. This means that from the elements that compose the live execution, i.e., from the composer, to the interpreter, to the audience, the room, the loudspeakers, ... are bind together, to form a structure, understood as the total is more than the sum of the parts. What bind together these elements is the continuity, given, in my compositional view, by the space as common element. The challenges I encountered were mainly technical, i.e., a correct implementation of a software part respect to the hardware components. During live execution, the difficulties are mainly provided to the interaction with the interpreter, within which I have to create a proper communication to ensure that a correct tuning is performed. Moreover, the execution of the pieces in different acoustical spaces is crucial, because some corrections can be performed even in the future while approaching a space that can escape from the provided framework. 
~~~

Integrating Spaces: Harnessing Tetrahedral Geometry in Spherical Loudspeaker Arrays for Bespoke Granular Synthesis

Abstract. This study introduces Campi Instabili, a pioneering exploration into sound synthesis that seamlessly integrates tetrahedral geometry within spherical loudspeaker arrays to transcend traditional auditory experiences. Leveraging a custom-developed granular synthesis technique executed through novel C++ software, this project redefines the dynamic interaction between sound production and spatial acoustics. Each performance is uniquely adapted to its environment through a live, pre-performance tuning process, enabling the alignment of the composition with the specific acoustic characteristics of the venue. This approach not only challenges conventional paradigms in sound synthesis but also reimagines the role of performers in acousmatic music, who actively engage as listeners and tuning agents within the performance space. The resulting compositions offer a tailored auditory experience that invites new avenues for creative expression and interaction in music technology and spatial audio design.

1 Introduction
In the evolving landscape of music technology, where technological advancements incessantly reshape creative practices, Campi Instabili pioneers a novel exploration that incorporates tetrahedral geometry within spherical loudspeaker arrays to challenge and enhance spatial auditory experiences. This project not only pushes the boundaries of conventional sound synthesis but integrates granular synthesis technique and spatial audio design to optimize acoustic interactions within varied performance spaces.

The introduction of a custom-developed C++ software bridges technological ingenuity with artistic inquiry, enabling a bespoke synthesization process that tailors soundscapes dynamically to the acoustical properties of each performance location. This shifts the conventional role of performers in acousmatic music to active participants who respond and adjust to their sonic environment, facilitating an immersive and adaptive auditory experience.

2 Conceptual Background and Theoretical Underpinnings
Campi Instabili is grounded in a speculative approach to sound synthesis that integrates computational technology with spacious audio design to explore new auditory experiences. This project not only redefines traditional compositional methodologies but also utilizes technology in ways that heighten the interactive experience between the sound and the space.

2.1 Speculative Sound Synthesis


The project challenges traditional sound synthesis paradigms by adopting a dynamic, responsive approach, where synthesis is not just a matter of sound generation but also a tool for spatial interaction and exploration. This approach leverages granular synthesis to manipulate sound textures and timbres dynamically, adjusted site-specifically according to the acoustical properties of the performance space. This method exemplifies how technological advancements can transform creative sound practices.

2.2 Interdisciplinary Integration

By integrating principles from acoustics and psychoacoustics, the project does not strictly focus on the technology of sound but also deeply considers how sound is perceived in different spatial configurations. The use of a bespoke spherical loudspeaker array, based on tetrahedral geometry, challenges the listener’s usual passive experience by actively reshaping soundscapes according to their movement and location within the space.

2.3 Reimagining Musical Composition

This project treats musical composition as a choreographic, adaptable interaction between hardware and the composer’s intent, where the final output is uniquely sensitive to its performed environment. Giorgio Netti and Agostino Di Scipio’s influences are evident as they promote the idea of sound not just filling space but interacting with it. Incorporating these theoretical insights ensures that Campi Instabili extends beyond a technical demonstration to pose important questions about the role and definition of musical composition in contemporary practices.
2.4 Contemporary Music Influences
Campi Instabili draws from a diverse array of influential composers who have each challenged conventional boundaries of musical composition and performance. For instance, Giorgio Netti’s exploration of the instrument as a tool to investigate space directly informs our approach to understanding and utilizing loudspeakers as active components that interact with their environment. Similarly, Gerard Grisey’s technique, particularly evident during a rehearsal at Villa Medici, where he adjusted the performance tempo of “Les espaces acoustiques” to accommodate the room’s reverberance, is mirrored in our method of pre-performance tuning to align the composition with the unique acoustics of each venue.

The project also encapsulates Agostino Di Scipio’s ideas of “Audible Ecosystemics”, which emphasize live electronic setups that evolve based on their interactions with the surrounding environment. This aligns with our use of site-specific, adaptive sound technology systems. Additionally, following John Cage’s philosophies that challenge preconceived notions of musical performance spaces and audience engagement, Campi Instabili promotes a dynamic interaction between the performance and the audience, each influencing the other.

Under Michelangelo Lupone’s guidance, particularly through his works like “Canto di Madre”, which utilize complex sound structures and advanded granular synthesis technique, Campi Instabili adopts a granular approach to synthesis that respects and responds to spatial characteristics, pushing the boundaries of traditional sound synthesis methods.
3 Design and Development

The design of Campi Instabili combines innovative sound synthesis techniques with custom-built hardware to optimize interactions within various performance spaces.

3.1 Hardware Integration

The S.T.One loudspeaker system utilizes a unique tetrahedral arrangement to maximize spatial sound dispersion, crucial for the immersive auditory experiences intended in this project. This setup allows precise control over sound placement and movement, essential for exploring spatial dynamics effectively.

3.2 Custom Granular Synthesis Development

At the core of the project is a specifically developed granular synthesis engine that integrates seamlessly with the spherical loudspeaker setup. This setup manipulates sound grains to construct complex auditory landscapes that respond dynamically to the immediate acoustic environment, showcasing a practical application of theoretical concepts in real-world settings.

3.3 Software Architecture

Utilizing object-oriented programming, the custom software architecture supports flexible, intuitive manipulation of sound parameters, proving essential for live performance adaptability. This setup not only reflects advanced programming practices but also the practical necessities of site-specific sound art performance.

3.4 Integrating the Listening Environment

The system’s design considers the unique acoustic properties of performance spaces, enabling pre-performance calibrations that fine-tune auditory outputs to specific environments. This feature situates the project within practical applications, ensuring that each performance is optimized for its specific location.

4 Aesthetic Consideration
The aesthetic framework of Campi Instabili centers on exploring new modalities of listening and comprehension within a space influenced by sound technology. This involves a critical engagement with sonic material, spatial characteristics of the environment, and the perceptual faculties of the audience.


4.1 Redefining Spatial Perception

The spatial arrangement in Campi Instabili invites the audience to experience sound as a choreographic, immersive environment rather than emanating from a localized source. This outer-radiating setup enhances the uncertainty between source and reflection, prompting listeners to navigate the space through auditory cues.

4.2 Sound Materiality and Synthesis

Using purely synthetic sine waves, the sound design focuses on the clarity and purity of tones, highlighting micro-variations that inform the spatial character of the sound. This approach emphasizes textural possibilities and the gestalt phenomena arising from microscopic sonic changes.

4.3 Interactive Composition and Performance

The integration of room acoustics into performance redefines the roles of composer and performer, advocating for a participatory role for performers akin to that of instrumentalists. This transforms the performance into a dynamic interaction between human and computational processes, where both are integral in shaping the auditory experience.

4.4 Audience as Part of the Performance Ecology

Each listener’s unique position within the space suggests a non-dominant acoustic field view, emphasizing an egalitarian approach to auditory experiences. This dynamic engagement encourages continuous renegotiation of auditory perspectives, actively constructing individual auditory experiences through movement and attention.

4.5 Challenging Conventional Aesthetic Experience

By merging sound art with technology, Campi Instabili questions traditional musical performance boundaries, engaging critically with the influence of technology on cultural perceptions of sound and space.
5 Analysis and Discussion
Campi Instabili manifests an innovative integration of computational sound design and site-specific acoustic adaptation, demonstrating how advanced technology can be harmoniously embedded in artistic practices. This project serves as a case study in utilizing speculative art to push the envelope in digital music performance, emphasizing the continuity between roles of composer, performer, and technology in creating immersive auditory experiences.

5.1 Technology and Space: A Symbiotic Relationship

The project exemplifies how spatial characteristics can actively shape and be shaped by computational sound technologies, illustrating a symbiotic relationship that enhances and personalizes the listener’s experience.

5.2 Rethinking Compositional Practice

Reflecting on the speculative nature of the composition, this intervention in traditional music making reveals new pathways for artistic expression where variability and adaptability become central elements.

5.3 Broader Implications

Ultimately, Campi Instabili not only challenges conventional auditory experiences but also encourages a broader discourse on the role of computational technologies in the future of sound art and music performances, suggesting possibilities for further interdisciplinary studies.

When applying, you need to fill out an online form, in which you describe the startup you intend to launch in Denmark. To determine whether your business is suitable for Startup Denmark, we need to know what startup you intend to launch. Provide a brief presentation as well as some general information. Keep it short, clear, and precise. Why will your startup be successful in Denmark? 

Product or service presentation 
We need to know the development stage of the product you intend to base your startup on, whether it is a service, an app, a robotic arm or something completely different. Is it still just an idea, have you developed a prototype or are you already in the market? 

Resources and competences in the business 
Not only do you need to come up with a great business plan, but you must also be capable of running a successful branch in practice. It is therefore important that you show that you have the skills, competences and experiences needed to turn your branch into a viable venture. When applying, you will need to tell us about the people behind your business. Why can you or your team launch a successful branch in Denmark?  It would also be relevant to describe the revenue/accounting of the foreign company so that the expert panel can see whether it is a healthy company or not. 

Market analysis and a sales or go-to-market strategy 
In your application you need to show us your market analysis and describe your sales or go-to-market strategy. Overall, it may contain:  

Market definition: Which markets will be targeted to sell the product or service?  
Competitors: Who are the competitors in the market? 
Customers: Who is the target audience within these markets? 
Distribution model: How will the product or service be delivered to the customer? 
Price: How much should the product or service cost for each customer group? 
Marketing: How will you reach your target customers and create demand?  
Why Denmark? 
You must describe why you want to launch your startup in Denmark. It may be specific opportunities that Denmark can create for your company, that you have business relations in Denmark or something else that makes Denmark the right country for you. 

Activities in the start-up phase 
You must describe what activities you plan to carry out to establish your startup in Denmark. 

It is recommended that you also insert an overall budget for your initial activities.

An article’s data availability statement lets a reader know where and how to access data that support the results and analysis. It may include links to publicly accessible datasets that were analysed or generated during the study, descriptions of what data are available and/or information on how to access data that is not publicly available.

The data availability statement is a valuable link between a paper’s results and the supporting evidence. Springer Nature’s data policy is based on transparency, requiring these statements in original research articles across our journals.

The guidance below offers advice on how to create a data availability statement, along with examples from different research areas.

What should a data availability statement include?
Your data availability statement should describe how the data supporting the results reported in your paper can be accessed. 

If your data are in a repository, include hyperlinks and persistent identifiers (e.g. DOI or accession number) for the data where available.  
If your data cannot be shared openly, for example to protect study participant privacy, then this should be explained. 
Include both original data generated in your research and any secondary data reuse that supports your results and analyses.

Citing data sources
You should cite any publicly available data on which the conclusions of the paper rely. This includes novel data shared alongside the publication and any secondary data sources. 

Data citations should include a persistent identifier (such as a DOI), should be included in the reference list using the minimum information recommended by DataCite (Dataset Creator, Dataset Title, Publisher [repository], Publication Year, Identifier [e.g. DOI, Handle or ARK]) and follow journal style."

RESIDENT, NON-DOMICILED COMPANIES
The scope of taxation in Malta depends on the person’s residence and domicile. In the Income Tax Act, a ‘person’ is defined as an individual and a body of persons which includes companies, any fellowship, society or other association of persons, whether corporate or unincorporated and whether vested with legal personality.

While the term ‘domicile’ is not defined in the Income Tax Acts, in the case of a body of persons, it is deemed to be the place of incorporation or principal seat of registration of the body of persons. A company which is registered in Malta is deemed to be domiciled and tax resident in Malta from the date of its incorporation, and is subject to a flat rate of 35% on its worldwide income[1]. This does not mean, however, that a Maltese company which operates abroad may never be taxed in that country. Cases of dual residence may arise, for instance when one State attaches importance to the place of incorporation whereas another attaches importance to the place of effective management.

A company incorporated outside of Malta is considered to be resident in Malta only if its place of effective management and control is in Malta. As a general rule, ‘the place of effective management’ is defined as the place where the key management and commercial decisions that are necessary for the conduct of the company’s business are in substance made. This is generally, though not necessarily, the place where the board of directors meet and resolve business.

Therefore, a company which is incorporated in Malta is considered to be resident and domiciled in Malta, while a company which is incorporated outside Malta but has its control and management in Malta will be considered as resident but not domiciled in Malta.

Companies which are resident but not domiciled (or vice versa) in Malta are subject to tax in Malta on all income and chargeable gains arising in Malta, and on income arising outside Malta which is remitted back to Malta. No tax is payable on foreign income which is not received in Malta and on capital gains arising outside Malta to a company which is not ordinarily resident and domiciled in Malta, even if remitted to Malta. On the other hand, companies which are neither incorporated nor resident in Malta are only chargeable on income and capital gains arising in Malta.

A company registered abroad that shifts its management and control seat to Malta is deemed to be resident, but not domiciled, in Malta and would be able to reap the fiscal advantages available to Malta resident companies. Such advantages include the application of the tax credit imputation mechanism and the tax refunds available to the shareholders of the company on a final distribution of dividends. These fiscal advantages are discussed further below.

Malta resident companies (even those not domiciled) are to allocate distributable profits to one or more of 5 tax accounts, depending on the nature and the source of the profits. These tax accounts are: the Foreign Income Account (FIA), the Maltese Taxed Account (MTA), the Final Tax Account (FTA), the Immovable Property Account (IPA), and the Untaxed Account (UA).

Full imputation system
Malta operates a full imputation system for dividends paid out from the prof­its of the company. Dividends are subject to tax in the hands of the shareholder however, shareholders receive a full imputation credit for the tax paid by the company. The full imputation system ensures that the shareholder is not subject to further tax on dividends distributed and therefore, eliminates economic double taxation.

Tax Refunds
Furthermore, the effective tax paid may be reduced through the application of various refunds available to the shareholders of a Malta resident company. Although often associated with the imputation system, the tax refund is over and above the imputation credit outlined above and is intended to reduce overall tax burden in Malta in the hands of the shareholder.

Available Tax Refunds in Malta:
100% Refund – Applies when profits are derived from a participating holding which qualifies for the participation exemption.
6/7ths Refund – This type of refund is generally due on those profits earned from trading activities. Taking into account such refund, the effective rate of tax works out at 5%.
5/7ths Refund – This type of refund is generally due in respect of income derived from passive interest and royalties and income from participating holdings which do not qualify for the participation exemption. The effect rate of tax works out at 10%.
2/3rds Refund – Available in those instances where the company has claimed double taxation relief. The refund depends on the type of double taxation relief availed of and is limited to the tax paid in Malta.
The participation exemption (or 100% refund) mentioned above applies to a Malta registered company which derives profits or gains from a participating holding in a non-resident entity. In such a case, the Malta holding company may decide:

either to apply an outright exemption from tax or
to include such income or gains as part of the taxable income of the Malta resident company and pay tax at the default rate of 35%. Following the distribution of dividends by the Malta resident company out of the said income or gains, the recipient shareholders would be entitled to a full (100%) refund of the tax paid by the company on such income or gains.
Withholding tax
Malta does not levy withholding tax on distributions of dividends to non-resident shareholders. Moreover, as long as certain conditions are met, Malta would not levy any withholding tax on payments of interest and royalties to persons not resident in Malta.

In summary, the benefits associated with resident, non-domiciled companies are:
Worldwide basis of taxation is not applicable to companies who are resident but not domiciled in Malta;
No tax is payable on foreign income which is not remitted to Malta
Capital gains remitted to Malta are not subject to any tax whatsoever;
Access to Malta’s wide treaty network as well as unilateral relief provisions.
Access to Malta’s full imputation system and tax refund system
[1] This means all income and capital gains wherever it arises and whether received in Malta or not.

2. Marketing and Market Entry Tactics:
- Localized Marketing Strategies: Although there are broad marketing strategies mentioned, localized tactics tailored to Danish culture and consumer behaviors could be more specifically outlined.
- Competitor Response Strategies: The plan might include anticipated competitor reactions and strategies to counteract these to retain a competitive edge.

3. Regulatory and Compliance Details:
- Detailed Compliance Roadmap: More comprehensive details about the step-by-step process of meeting regulatory requirements in Denmark, potential hurdles, and timeline specifics.

- Talent Acquisition and Retention Plans: More detailed strategies on attracting top talent and retaining them, especially in competitive fields like AI and health technology.

- User Onboarding Experience: Detailed walkthroughs of the user journey from onboarding to regular use, which can showcase the user-centric design focus.
- Engagement Metrics: Pre-launch engagement strategies or metrics from pilot programs that indicate user interest and potential retention rates.

8. Impact Measurement:
- Social Impact Metrics: More granular metrics on how the platform intends to measure social impact, particularly in underprivileged communities.
- Environmental Impact Report: A detailed study or future commitments on reducing the environmental impact, especially relevant given the global push towards sustainability.

Assistant: As an experienced Financial Analyst, I understand that combining technical analysis with fundamental analysis can provide a comprehensive view of potential investment opportunities, especially in sectors like technology, banking, and AI. Let’s break down the analysis process using the provided tools and objectives.  
  
\### Technical Analysis Tools  
  
1\. **Simple Moving Average (SMA)**:  
\- **Short-term (20-day SMA)**: Monitor this for signals regarding short-term trends in stock prices. For instance, if the price crosses above the SMA, it can indicate a potential buying opportunity.  
\- **Long-term (200-day SMA)**: A long-term measure is crucial for identifying the overall trend. If the stock is trading above the 200-day SMA, it’s generally considered bullish.  
  
2\. **Relative Strength Index (RSI)**:  
\- An RSI above 70 indicates that a stock might be overbought, while below 30 suggests it could be oversold. For aggressive investors, buying when the RSI is low and selling when it hits the high can yield returns.  
  
3\. **Fibonacci Retracement**:  
\- This tool is useful for identifying potential reversal levels in stock prices. By drawing retracement levels on a prior significant move, you can identify areas of support and resistance.  
  
\### Fundamental Analysis Methods  
  
1\. **Financial Statement Analysis**:  
\- **Income Statement**: Focus on revenue growth, particularly in the technology and AI sectors, where innovation drives profitability.  
\- **Balance Sheet**: Analyze the debt levels in banks and tech companies. A low debt-to-equity ratio can indicate stability.  
\- **Cash Flow Statement**: Positive cash flow is essential for growth opportunities in tech companies. Look for consistent cash generation.  
  
\### Macroeconomic Environment Considerations  
  
1\. **Interest Rates**: Low interest rates can benefit technology and AI sectors, as it lowers borrowing costs and encourages investment. Conversely, rising rates may impact the banking sector negatively.  
  
2\. **Inflation**: High inflation can affect consumer spending but can also lead to higher prices for services and products. Understanding the inflation environment can help predict the performance of banks (higher interest margins) versus technology (potentially stifled demand).  
  
3\. **Global Events**: Monitor geopolitical risks and global economic indicators (like GDP growth, unemployment rates, etc.) that can impact economic stability.

How to Convert Your Transaction History into CoinTracker-Compatible CSV Format
This guide will walk you through the process of formatting your exchange's CSV to the CoinTracker format to import in cases where automatic syncing or custom file import are not available.

If you are troubleshooting errors after attempting to import your formatted CSV, check out this guide instead: Troubleshooting CSV Import Errors in CoinTracker

What is the purpose of the CoinTracker CSV format?
CoinTracker integrates with a wide array of blockchains, exchanges, and wallets directly. However, in scenarios where automatic syncing is unavailable or a bug disrupts the process, manually importing transactions via CSV files becomes necessary.

CoinTracker simplifies this by supporting direct uploads of transaction history CSV files from exchanges or wallets whenever possible, eliminating the need for modifications. In cases where importing the unedited CSV file isn't possible, converting your exchange's transaction history CSV file into CoinTracker's format is required for successful import.

How to Format Your Transaction History CSV to the CoinTracker Format
Step 1: Export Your Transaction History
First, we'll need your transaction data from the exchange or wallet: 

Navigate to the exchange or wallet you wish to add to CoinTracker.
Seek the option for exporting transaction history, usually available as a CSV file. If you do not see this option, please contact the exchange or wallet to ask if it is available.
Step 2: Prepare Your CSV for CoinTracker
Download our CSV template —this contains the correct headers you will need to reformat your CSV. You can add your transactions into the template or use it as a guide.
Headers: The headers must match the template exactly:
Column A	Column B	Column C	Column D	Column E	Column F	Column G	Column H
Date	Received Quantity	Received Currency	Sent Quantity	Sent Currency	Fee Amount	Fee Currency	Tag
Columns: Can be in any order but all must be present—do not delete or add columns.
Step 3: Put the Right Information in Each Column
Now, you’ll need to add all the data you have from your existing CSV to the template you’ve downloaded:

Date and Time
Columns:

Date (Column A): The exact date and time of the transaction.
Date and Time Format:  MM/DD/YYYY HH:MM:SS. For example, "06/14/2017 20:57:35".

Time entries are optional. If you choose to include a time, it is assumed to be in UTC. If your time data is in another timezone, ensure you convert it to UTC before entry to guarantee accuracy. 
Sent and Received Assets
Columns:

Received Quantity (Column B): The amount of crypto or fiat you have received. 
Received Currency (Column C): This is the type of crypto you have received.
Sent Quantity (Column D): This is the amount of crypto or fiat currency you sent.
Sent Currency (Column E): This is the type of crypto you have sent.
Fee Amount (Column F) This is the amount of the transaction fee in the currency it was paid in.
Fee Currency (Column G): This is the type of currency that your transaction fee was paid in.
Quantity Format: Numbers only, including decimals if applicable. For example, "1.05". Do not include text other than numbers.

Currency Format: The token symbol of the received crypto. For example, "BTC" or "USD".

Other Considerations:

Blank Cells: If no data exists, leave the cell blank. Here are some examples of transaction types that will have blank cells:
Staking rewards will only have received data—'Sent Quantity' and 'Sent Currency' will be blank.
Transfers to another wallet will have only sent data—'Received Quantity' and 'Received Currency' will be blank.
See more in the Examples section at the end of this article
Currency Symbols: Only currencies supported by CoinTracker will be accepted. You may see an error if an unsupported currency is used in the file. You can check if your currency is supported and, if not, use this guide to create a custom currency, which can then be used in your CSV: How to Create a Custom Currency
Pairs: If your trade is expressed as a trading pair, be sure to split the token symbols according to the transaction type.
Transaction Category Tags 
Column

Tag (Column H): To categorize transactions by type for better tracking and tax purposes. This column is optional.
Tag Format: Only certain CoinTracker CSV tags will be accepted by the importer—any other text will cause the import to fail or ignore the row containing an unsupported tag. Make sure the text exactly matches one of the available 'CoinTracker CSV Tags' listed in this help article: Transaction Category Definitions.

Other Considerations:

When to Use Tags: Tags help categorize transactions correctly for tax purposes and portfolio tracking. Without tags, transactions imported via CSV default to Sent, Received, Trade, or Transfer (when the wallet transferred to or from is also added to CoinTracker). Tagging allows you to specify transaction types for Sent and Received transactions. You can add tags in Column H before import or update categories manually after import using this guide: How to Change a Transaction Category.
Not for All Transactions: You cannot tag trades or transfers and you should not use tags unless it is necessary to categorize a transaction.
Use Supported Tags Only: Only certain tags are accepted. Incorrect tags will cause import issues, including import failure and incorrectly tagged rows to be missing after import.
Transaction Memo: This column cannot be used for memos or notes. You can leave a note on a transaction after import by editing the transaction.
Step 4: Upload Your CSV to CoinTracker
Save the file as .csv file type.
Import your CSV file to the CoinTracker CSV import page.
Demos of CSV Reformatting
For a written walkthrough of how a CSV is converted to the Cointracker-compatible format, check out this article: How to Import FTX US Transactions via CSV

Your task is to systematically analyze, optimize, and transform the original prompt, ensuring it meets the following objectives: maximal semantic depth, precision in expression, and contextual adaptability across diverse use cases.

Process Guidelines:

Contextual Objective Extraction:

Identify the latent and overt objectives embedded within the user-provided prompt, including implied goals, nuanced expectations, and potential ambiguities.
Decompose the prompt into semantic components, exploring hidden relationships and dependencies between terms, entities, and underlying structures.
Consider edge cases, context shifts, and potential misinterpretations that may arise when different levels of expertise or domain knowledge are applied to the prompt.
Semantic Layering and Enrichment:

Construct multiple, semantically rich alternative versions of the prompt. Each version should probe the depths of meaning, context, and search intent while incorporating both explicit and latent elements of the user’s needs.
Account for complex edge cases, such as multi-domain relevance, shifts in language tone or audience, and the intended outcome in various hypothetical scenarios.
For each alternative, consider how varying degrees of specificity, abstraction, or detail could impact the prompt’s effectiveness in addressing multifaceted objectives.
Optimization Through Iterative Refinement:

Apply gradient-based techniques to test and evaluate alternative prompts, ensuring each iteration moves closer to an ideal balance of clarity, semantic richness, and relevance to the task at hand.
Assess each version’s adaptability across varying contexts, edge cases, or domain-specific nuances, while maintaining coherence with the user’s initial intent.
Explore and resolve potential ambiguities or gaps in knowledge that may reduce the prompt’s ability to generalize across multiple expert-level or domain-specific applications.
Comprehensive Evaluation and Final Optimization:

Synthesize the most optimized and contextually precise version of the prompt, integrating insights gained through iterative refinement.

Objective: Take a traditional ed-tech program and transform it into an artificially intelligent interface which allows users to absorb program content, practice code, get active feedback, engage in exercises and activities within the interface.

Context: We have a program on Solana development. We designed a custom LMS which is broadly divided into 5 parts. On the very left side of the page we have a nav bar wherein users can set up their account information (name, photo, personal information) wherein users can watch the video library. Each video has reference materials which are accessible under a drop down menu button under each video. On right side we have an option panel which has 3 buttons, a video button which shows you a list of videos yet to watch (like a YouTube video list) and an ‘exercises’ button and an ‘activities’ wherein you click on the buttons to find the number of exercises and activities the user has unlocked on the basis of videos the user has watched.
Below the video we have a description and under the description we have a ‘doubts’ section which is basically a comment section wherein users can post a doubt and one of our tutors will manually reply back.
A very traditional system.

User problems:
1. They need to feel that they have access to support 24/7 whenever they need it.
2. Live 1 on 1 sessions, for the same reason of having support whenever they need it
3. Retention issues because without enough motivation binge watching program videos can become boring

Current platform issues
1. Very clunky user experience: The videos are great but access to reference materials and especially the way ‘exercises and activities’ get unlocked are not ‘intuitive’. A notifications icon appears on the exercises and activities button prompting users to click. 
2. The overall experience feels very traditional ‘ed-tech’-ish which generally gets a bad rap.
3. The doubt section is completely manual which can become overwhelming for the tutors to respond to in time.

Envisioned solution:
1. Imagine an artificially intelligent platform which is trained on the entire program
2. Instead of ‘binge watching video, separate doubt section, separate exercises and activities section’, the entire program becomes a running conversation
3. The program shall begin with first understanding the education, aptitude and cognition levels of the users. Preferably a voice integration in the system will help to provide a human feel. 
4. The user should be able to toggle between voice mode and text mode.
5. The interface should be follow the same trajectory as the program, the system should tell the user to go through these references, ask user to perform exercises and tasks as the user reaches the commensurate level of proficiency.
6. Active doubt solving support 24/7.
7. The user should be able to bookmark messages for future references.

Assistant: In the early stages of your startup, it’s common for the founder to take on multiple roles and responsibilities, so choosing an appropriate job title can be a bit nuanced. Here are some suggestions for both your initial title and how to approach titles as your team grows:  
  
\### Initial Job Title:  
1\. **Founder**: This is a common title for someone who has started the company and is versatile across different areas. It captures your ownership and leadership role without being too formal.  
2\. **Founder & Lead Developer**: Since you’re handling software development initially, you could include a specific functional aspect of your role.  
3\. **Founder & General Manager**: This reflects both your leadership and operational roles in the startup.  
  
\### When You Hire More Staff:  
As your team grows and you begin to hire additional staff, you can start to formalize roles and titles:  
  
1\. **Engineering Roles**:  
\- **Software Developer/Engineer**: For those directly involved in software creation.  
\- **Systems Administrator**: For someone managing and overseeing IT systems and infrastructure.  
\- **Network Administrator/Engineer**: For someone focused on network-related responsibilities.  
  
2\. **Your Transition**:  
\- As you step back from direct technical work, you can transition to a title like **CEO** or **Chief Executive Officer**. This signifies your role in leading the company, setting its strategic direction, and managing the broader aspects of the business, such as marketing and finance.  
  
3\. **Other Emerging Roles**:  
\- Eventually, as you grow, consider roles like **CTO (Chief Technology Officer)** for someone leading the technical direction or **COO (Chief Operating Officer)** if you find someone to manage daily operations.  
  
\### Tips:
